[The *Bodhāyanāhnika*, the section on daily rites (*nityakarmapariccheda*) composed by Pañcākṣaranātha, [and] the *Bodhāyanamantrapraśna*. (p2. nil) (the same title at p3a.
I bow to the god Vināyaka, to Madeva, to the auspicious Śivā,
to Vāṇī, and also to Mahāviṣṇu, the bestower of protection and the attainment of goals.
The daily, occasional, and optional rites, distinguished by various paths,
cause delusion for all twice-born ones, even for those who are learned.
Having understood that [work] by Bodhāyana and others in brief,
I— the Guru Pañcākṣara— shall speak for the enlightenment of even the ignorant this *Karmaprakāśikā*, which distinguishes between the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.

Having risen at a time five *nāḍikās* prior to sunrise, having washed his feet and hands, having smeared himself with ashes, and having meditated upon his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), he should depart from his house with his staff and other requisites. Having gone to a place outside the village and set aside his staff and other items in one spot, he should proceed to a location not frequented by spirits such as the *Nairṛta*, and so forth— where *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and the like [do not dwell].
All the deities, the ṛṣis, and likewise the lords of the Gaṇas.
I create suspicion here; therefore, let them go far away from this place.
During the day and at the two twilights, one should face north; at night, one should face south.

At times when there is danger to life and so forth, one should comfortably wrap the head, wear the sacred thread over the right ear, remain silent, cover the ground with grass and the like, and void excrement there. Then, having wiped the anus with wood or similar material, grasping the penis with the left hand and taking the previously collected earth with the other hand, one should go to the bank of water not intended for bathing and perform purification in that manner. In the absence of such a place, one should take earth from the water, deposit it nearby, and [proceed].

One should perform purification. Having cleansed the penis with water using a single application of clay the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit, one should first cleanse the anus with the application of half a handful (*prasṛti*) of clay; then a second [handful]... [of clay]... having cleansed [the anus] with water in the absence of clay, and having repeatedly cleansed the penis or the left hand in the intervals, one should afterwards cleanse both seven times. Afterwards, having performed the purification of the body, one should perform the purification of the mind (*bhāva*). [This is] purification...

[He] should cause [the water] to flow away. In the absence of water, having extracted [the wood], he should perform purification as before. Afterwards, having cleansed his feet three times each and his hands once, and having performed the cleansing of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water, he should sip water (*ācamana*) while reciting: "O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge (*brahman*), wisdom, and intelligence. Having said this, he should take up a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) that is not during a forbidden lunar day (*parvan*), straight, ten finger-breadths in length, and made of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, or similar materials; however, [wood from] the *palāśa* tree and others should be avoided.

Having adopted another [method], one should avoid [the practice] on the first, sixth, eighth, ninth, eleventh, fourteenth, and other such days; on other days, however, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth. One should always use grass or leaves, except on the new moon day (*amāvāsya*) and the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*);
yet even on those two days, one may do so with leaves of the *jambu*, *plakṣa*, or mango trees.
On days such as those for ancestral rites (śrāddha), one should perform the purification of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
[Now, the bath.]

One should perform the recitation of the *saṅkalpasūkta*, the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and the libations to the gods and others. (…) (l6. The characteristics of the five-fold [rite]: Having extracted five lumps of clay from rivers and other such places and having placed them on the bank, [one says]: "Whether impure or pure, O [Name], on this auspicious lunar day, for the sake of the destruction of my accumulated sins and for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord who is the gateway [to liberation], I shall perform the morning bath. (p4b., f2a. l1. The waters are the forms of all deities, and they are the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses.

O Lords of the Earth, I bow to you; I shall bathe in you for the sake of complete purification. To him in whose hair are the clouds, in whose joints are all the rivers, and in whose belly are the oceans—to that Lord, [I offer] my salutation. O Support of the entire world, grant me this permission from the gods to resort to your sacred bathing places (tīrtha).
[She who is] exceedingly fierce, of massive form, and like the fire at the end of an aeon—
Salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should deign to grant me permission.

Then one should consecrate the water with the following mantra: "Water indeed is all this; water is all beings; water is the vital breaths... water is the purifier; water is immortality; water is the sovereign (*samrāj*); water is the radiant ruler (*virāj*); water is the self-ruling lord (*svarāj*); water is the meters; water is the luminous powers; water is all the deities; water is *bhūr*, *bhuvas*, and *suvas*; water is *om*. May the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the oceans, the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) such as Puṣkara, and all other holy bathing places be present for me at the time of bathing. Having thus recollected all the sacred fords, one should bathe. Now follows the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra:

I take refuge in Varuṇa of golden horns; may he purify my place of pilgrimage. Whatever I have eaten that was unwholesome, whatever acceptance of gifts from the wicked, and whatever evil deed I have committed with my mind, speech, or body—may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that for me again and again. Thus, offer [the water] with cupped hands.

"May the waters and plants be friendly to us; may they be auspicious to us. May he who hates us and whom we hate be struck down. Then, having sipped water, [one says]: "Homage to Agni who dwells in the waters; homage to Indra; homage!"

"Salutation to Varuṇa, salutation to Vāruṇī, salutations to the waters. Thus he pays homage. He circumambulates three times to the right and turns the water around [himself]. "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart! Whatever is other than this, non-terrible, and fierce—that King Varuṇa shall wipe away with his hand. May I, sinless, stainless, released, and freed from blemish, having ascended to the back of the firmament, go to the world of Brahman. "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī... [and so on].

Having entered the water at the bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the verses: "The Śutudrī with its pure banks, the Paruṣṇī with its dark waters, the Asiknī, the Vitastā, the Arjīkī, and those [rivers] which flow into the Sraṇuhī," he purifies himself with water. Having performed the purification with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed refreshing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ*), with the four verses beginning "Golden-colored and pure" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*), and with this entire section beginning "Pavamāna, who dwells in the light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*), [he recites]: "Order (*ṛta*) and Truth (*satya*) were born from fervor (*tapas*); from that the night was born, and from that the billowing ocean."

From the ocean, the vast sea, the year was born; from him, as he willed, came days and nights and the manifold universe. Dhātṛ fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before, and likewise the heaven, the earth, the mid-air, and the light of heaven. Whatever sin is upon the earth, in the dust, or in the atmosphere, across the two worlds—may you, O Varuṇa, purify these waters, you who wash away transgression. He is the one who looks upon this world, the guardian of the universe; he [leads] the worlds of the doers of merit; he [sees] the golden [world] beyond death. [He pervades] heaven and earth.

I have taken refuge in the golden heaven; I have sharpened my golden essence. The moist light blazes—I am that light. The light blazes—I am Brahman. Whatever I am, I am Brahman. I alone am I; I offer myself—*svāhā*. Whether one has committed an improper act, been incontinent, a thief, a killer of an embryo, or violated the teacher’s bed—one is released from that sin through the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn dedicated to Varuṇa. [Section on Bathing and Libations] Dust... (p5b., f3a., sideheading: *snānatarpaṇam*)... l1.

"The wise proclaim me as the Earth-praise (*bhūmistava*): 'May the Ṛṣis purify [me], may the Vasus purify [me], may Varuṇa purify [me], may Aghamarṣaṇa purify [me]'—reciting this while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins. [Reciting] 'As if released from the pillar' (*drupadādiva mumucānaḥ*) or 'Bathed, stainless, and pure' (*snātvī malādiva*), may the waters purify my mind"—having immersed oneself three times in the water, one should recite these three verses. "Let the Great Lord of All (*viśveśa*), the destroyer of Tripura, Śrīkaṇṭha, whose bow is Mount Meru, Hara, the remover of sin, be worshipped. Salutations to our gurus."

"I am liberated from the [sins] of those who wear the form of a *sāman*... Having bathed thus three times, one should bathe. [... Having returned and sipped water (*ācamya*), one should say: "I shall perform the ritual bathing and libation (*tarpaṇa*). I offer libations to the Vasus; I offer libations to the Rudras; I offer libations to the Ādityas; I offer libations to the Sādhyas; I offer libations to those beginning with Brahmā [...

I offer libations to all the gods; I offer libations to all the goddesses; I offer libations to all the wives of the hosts of gods; I offer libations to all the sons of the hosts of gods; I offer libations to all the grandsons of the hosts of gods; and to all...

The wives of the hosts of gods … Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and the other sages—those sages I satiate. All the sages I satiate. All the wives of the hosts of sages I satiate. All the sons of the hosts of sages I satiate. All the grandsons of the hosts of sages … the lords of the hosts of sages … Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder: Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Yama accompanied by the Aṅgirases, Agni Kavyavāhana and the others—those ancestors I satiate. All the ancestors I satiate. All the hosts of ancestors I satiate.

I satiate all the hosts of ancestors, [their] sons, and [their] grandsons; and I satiate all the wives of the hosts of ancestors. Carrying strength, nectar, ghee, milk, honey, and flowing libation—*svadhā*—may they satiate my ancestors;

may you satiate them, may you satiate them! Having thus repeated this three times with joined palms (*añjali*), [one offers] water. [Then one says: "The water defiled by that [act], for the purification of that sin, [is offered] to Yakṣman, along with pure accumulations of water."

I satisfy [the ancestors]. Having come to the bank and sitting down facing south, having emerged from the water while still wet, being pure and intent on auspicious food, for the sake of the pure ones who are pure—[reciting] the mantra:

"By the *ṛta* they have come to truth, they whose covenant is the *ṛta*, those of pure birth, pure, purifying"—he sprinkles the garment. Then, [reciting] the mantra: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee," he takes up the garment. [He recites: "The Rakṣas is driven away, the enemies are driven away; thou art the skin of Aditi... [and so on] until "...driven away."

Having shown the Sun—the god Jātavedas, whose rays are for all to see—[with the mantra] "The rays [reveal] Sūrya for all to behold," they bring [the water] forward, making it more abundant. [He should wear] his own garment... always during inhalation and exhalation. Then, having brought me prosperity... having put on armor, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he should sprinkle his wet garment, wash it in water, lift it out, wash it again, and then, having folded it fourfold... he should wring out the water. Those who are born in our family, the childless... the offspring.

"May those who have died accept this water squeezed from my cloth which I have given. Having said this, he should squeeze [the cloth], place it on his left forearm, and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice. Then, having gone to a body of water, sitting with the *pavitra* grass in hand, he should perform the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*) and the application of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍradhāraṇa*) according to the rules; having made the request, he should perform them with the five mantras beginning with *praśāna*. Then, having performed three rounds of *ācamana* with the *praṇava*, he should touch his lips with the base of his thumb.

Having wiped the mouth twice and sipped water, one should touch the two nostrils with the middle and thumbs, the two eyes with the ring fingers and thumbs, the two ears with the little fingers and thumbs, the two shoulders with the palms, and the navel and heart with all the fingers; one should touch the head with all [the fingers] silently in every case. That [is] the sipping of water (ācamana) performed with the syllable *oṃ*. Or it may be done with the *vyāhṛtis*, or even with the *Sāvitrī*; or it may be performed without mantras, as for the *praṇava*.

Because it was mentioned first, one should perform the daily rite (*nityakarman*) by that very [method]. Vṛddha-Śaṅkha says: One should sip water three times; then one should wipe the two lips with the root of the thumb. Then one should touch the mouth. By joining the index finger and the thumb, one should touch the two nostrils. Then, by joining the middle finger and the thumb, one should touch the two eyes.

By joining the ring finger and the thumb, one should touch the two ears. Then, by joining the little finger and the thumb, one should touch the two shoulders. And likewise, one should touch the navel and the heart.

One should touch [the body] with the palm of the hand; then, having performed this entire remaining rite of sipping water (*ācamana*), one should restrain the breath (*prāṇāyāma*) and say: "O Supreme Lord, the means for the destruction of my accumulated sins, I shall perform the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥsandhyopāsana*). Regarding the mantra *Āpo hiṣṭhā*: Sindhudvīpa is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*); Water is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sprinkling of water. "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss; grant us strength for our great delight and for the sake of vision. (p7a., f4b., l1. He who...

"May he be most auspicious to us; may we partake of his favor today, as longing mothers [partake of their sons]. To him may we go for refuge"—with these words, one sprinkles the seven heads. "For whose dwelling you quicken," with this, [one sprinkles] the two feet. "O Waters, give birth to us also," with this, there is sprinkling on the head as well. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ*, thus [one sprinkles] oneself.

For the *anuvāka* beginning with "Sūryaś ca," Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consumption of water. "Sūrya and I, and others, and the lords of wrath..."

May they protect me from sins committed out of anger. Whatever sin I have committed during the night—by means of mind, speech, hands, feet, belly, or genitals—may the Night wipe that away. Whatever misfortune is in me, this I cast into the Sun, the light whose source is immortality; *svāhā*. Having thus consumed water and then rinsed the mouth twice, one recites the mantra beginning with *dadhikrāviṇṇo akāriṣam*. Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*), and Dadhikrāvan is the deity (*devatā*). This is for the purification of the waters.

The application (*viniyoga*): "I have drawn [the essence] from Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse; he has made my mouth fragrant; may he prolong my life. "O Waters, you are most healing... (*āpo hiṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ*) ... "from good to better" (*suvassuvaḥ*). Thus, as before, I shall perform the offering of the *arghya*. For the mantra of the *arghya* offering, Viśvāmitra Gautama and Viśiṣṭha are the seers (*ṛṣis*);

the *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, and *anuṣṭubh* are the meters (*chandāṃsi*); Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the deities (*devatās*). [The *arghya* offering... Meditation on the Sun: His essence is ninefold, supreme...

[Visualizing] the light [of the sun], which is beyond the root... beyond the supreme... situated at the end of the circle of beings, the cause for the single discharge of the thousandfold thunderbolt-weapon; meditating upon the Supreme Self, one should cast [the water] that has never been offered before. (l. 2) *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. *Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.

Having thus extracted three handfuls of water (*arghya*) to the height of the tips of the ears, one should pour them into slightly stirred water. "I shall perform the *arghya* for expiation. *Oṃ bhūḥ*. *Oṃ bhuvaḥ*. *Oṃ*.

*Svaḥ*. *Oṃ* *mahaḥ*. *Oṃ* *janaḥ*. *Oṃ* *tapaḥ*. *Oṃ* *satyam*. *Oṃ* from *nat*. *Oṃ* *satyam*, *Oṃ* *tapaḥ*, *Oṃ* *janaḥ*, *Oṃ* *mahaḥ*, *Oṃ* *suvaḥ*, *Oṃ* *bhuvaḥ* (...). For the Brahmāstra mantra, Vasiṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), and Brahmā is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of destroying Asuras and Rākṣasas.

Having filled [the vessel] with water with "Oṃ raum," one offers the respectful oblation (*arghya*) with: "Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyam bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Parorajasi sāvadom. Ravom. Ravyom. Ravyo'ham."

For the mantra of the withdrawal of the weapon (*astrasaṃhāra*), the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the portion of Savitṛ belonging to the *brahmagāyatrī*. The meter (*chandas*) is the Goddess Gāyatrī. The deity (*devatā*) is the triple-formed (*trayīmūrti*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the withdrawal of the weapon. "I am he; I am the Sun, I am the light, the remover of the light of the Sun, the auspicious one. This is the self-light, the pure (*śukra*); this is all-light, I am he. (…) (Sandhyāvandana, p. 8a, f. 5b, sideheading) "O Sun, O Sun, I am [the Sun]. In the morning, you are Hara; know my evil. At midday, you are Udvarga; [know] my evil..."

"Know me. At evening, having performed the *saṃyuddha* [salutation], say: "Know my evil. Having muttered: "That which is the leader of speech, that which is upon this speech, may it protect the cattle... [and] "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he returns to the dwelling, circumambulates himself with the thought, "This sun is Brahman," touches his heart, sips water three times, and offers libations: "I satisfy Āditya; I satisfy Soma; I satisfy Aṅgāraka; I satisfy Budha; I satisfy Bṛhaspati..."
I offer libations to [the Sun]; I offer libations to Śukra; I offer libations to Śanaiścara; I offer libations to Rāhu; I offer libations to Ketu. Having sipped water as before:

*namaḥ* to Brahmā. *Brahmārpaṇam*. Having come to the bank: of this great mantra of the venerable Sandhyā-vandana, Sāndīpinī is the venerable seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*), Brahmā is the deity (*devatā*), the nine-fold face of drying (*śoṣaṇa*) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), ... is the power (*śakti*), the three eyes are the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation (*bhoga-mokṣa*).

The ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*): Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Uṃ Kliṃ Ta(+), salutation to the two index fingers. Maṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the two middle fingers. Aṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Uṃ Kliṃ, salutation to the two little fingers. Maṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. The ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*): Aṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the heart. Uṃ Kliṃ, *svāhā* to the head. Maṃ Sauḥ, *vauṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Aṃ Aiṃ, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*). Uṃ Kliṃ, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes. Aṃ Sauḥ, [salutation] to the weapon (*astra*).

Phaṭ! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ oṃ. For the sake of the desired twilight rite, [I meditate upon] the beautiful Nīlagrīvā, whose hands bestow boons and fearlessness, who has three eyes and the moon as her crest-jewel.
The root mantra: *aṃ heṃ uṃ kliṃ maṃ sau*. Having recited this sixteen times, one offers salutation:
"O highly fortunate one, homage to you who are worshipped by all the gods!
Merely by worshipping you, one is liberated from all sins."
That twilight is the form of the universe, transcending illusion and perfectly immovable;
she is the Sovereign, the source of the three [worlds],
O Sarasvatī, the great, multiform, and divine twilight!
Having recited the Praṇava, the Supreme Self—which is ageless, immortal, eternal, born of itself, and praised by Niṣa—with devotion, (l. 4).
One should meditate upon one's own true nature and prostrate on the ground like a staff.

Having returned to the place of recitation, one should offer salutations, saying: "Homage, constant homage to those twice-born gods who dwell from the world of Brahmā down to the very end of the worlds, as far as the Lokaparvata.
Thus, having offered salutation.
"May those beings depart who stand as obstacles;
may those beings who create hindrances go away by the command of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, he sat down and, with the sole of his left foot, made three marks on the ground.
For the sake of pacification, one should meditate on Viṣṇu wearing white garments.
These fierce spirits, piśācas, and others are indeed the stealers of the earth;
one should begin [the rite] for them while established in the Brahmakastha [mantra].

For the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*), Meru-peak is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chandaḥ*), the hand is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the seat. O Goddess of the world, you are the earth; you are supported by Viṣṇu. O Goddess, support me and make this seat pure.

Prāṇāyāma: Having grasped the nose with the thumb, the ring finger, and the little finger, and having bent the index and middle fingers, one should fill the external air through the left nostril for the duration of twelve *mātrās*. Holding the breath motionless for that same duration, one should exhale the air through the right [nostril] for that same duration. This is one *prāṇāyāma*. In this same manner, there is a second and a third. During the first retention (*kumbhaka*), one should recite "Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ... [and so on] three times. During the second retention...

Four times during the third *kumbhaka*. Having thus recited the *Gāyatrī* ten times along with the *Vyāhṛtis* and the *Śiras*, one then begins the recitation (*japa*). For a capable practitioner performing it in this manner, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *Praṇava* is Brahmā; the meter (*chandas*) is the Goddess Gāyatrī; the deity (*devatā*) is [Brahmā]; and its application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation. Having recited "Oṃ bhūḥ bhuvaḥ" ten times, [one proceeds]. For the section beginning with "Āyātu," the seer is Vāmadeva; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Gāyatrī; and its application is in invocation (*āvāhana*).

The Application (*viniyoga*): May the boon-granting Goddess come, together with the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and Brahman; O Gāyatrī, Mother of the meters, may you graciously accept this sacred prayer (*brahman*). You are vigor, you are endurance, you are strength, you are splendor;

you are the abode of the gods, you are named Viśva, you are the All, you are the Life of the All. You are everything, you are the Life of all, you are the Overcomer. *Oṃ*, I invoke Gāyatrī; I invoke Sāvitrī; I invoke Sarasvatī. Thus, in due order, at the morning, midday, and evening twilight prayers, [one should meditate] everywhere within the heart. Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the Sāvitrī.

(l3. *Nicara* is the *gāyatrī* metre; Savitṛ is the deity. (…) *Ṇiṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *yaṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *yāt* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining success through the grace of the *Gāyatrī* during recitation (*japa*). *Tatsavitur*, to Brahmā, with the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*): *namaḥ*. *Vareṇya*, to Viṣṇu-ātman, with the two index fingers (*tarjanī*): *namaḥ*. (l4. *Bhargo devasya*, to Rudra-ātman, with the two middle fingers (*madhyamā*): *namaḥ*. *Dhīmahi*, to Īśvara-ātman, with the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*): *namaḥ*. *Dhiyo yo naḥ*, to Sadāśiva-ātman, with the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*): *namaḥ*.
"May [the Lord] impel [me], O Self of All! Homage to the palms and the backs of the hands. Thus is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
The meditation (*dhyāna*):
with three eyes that possess the lusters of pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white...

I worship Gāyatrī, who is joined with the crescent moon bound upon her crown, whose complexion is the color of ultimate reality, and who carries in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a goad, a whip, a white skull-bowl,
a cord, a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses.

*Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ. Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyam, bhargo devasya dhīmahi, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* Having thus recited this one hundred and eight times while keeping the nose straight, and having repeated the *paryanta-aṣṭaka*, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) as before. (L2. For the *anuvāka* beginning with "uttame," Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Gāyatrī is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*). "O Goddess, on the highest peak upon the earth, you who cause the mountains to grow; having granted permission to the Brāhmaṇas, go forth, O Goddess."

"As you please: I shall perform the morning worship of the Sun. For the mantra beginning with 'Of Mitra' (*mitrasya*), Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the *hirug-gāyatrī* is the meter (*chanda*); Mitra is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is in the act of worship. Then, having risen and joined the palms in reverence: "The glory of the divine Mitra, who is established in the wide-seeing [heaven], is victorious; it is truth, possessed of wonderful renown. Mitra, knowing [all] as he knows the people, has supported the earth and the sky. Mitra gazes upon the tribes with unblinking eyes; for him we shall offer this oblation accompanied by clarified butter."* *The mantra continues:* *mitrasya carṣaṇī dhṛtaḥ śravo devasya sānasim | satyaṃ citraśravastamam ||* *mitro janān yātayati bruvāṇo mitro dādhāra pṛthivīm uta dyām | mitraḥ kṛṣṭīranimiṣābhicaṣṭe miterdayate vayo asmai ||* *asya havyaṃ ghṛtavat vidhema ||* [End of section 3 and 4.]*

May the mortal who offers oblations have a peaceful friend; O Āditya, he who exerts himself according to his vow is not slain and is not conquered. Protected by you, neither from near nor from afar does the wicked one reach him. Om, salutation to Sandhyā. Om, salutation to Sāvitrī. Om, salutation to Gāyatrī. Om, salutation to Sarasvatī. Salutation to all deities. Having said, "Desire has acted, anger has acted;
salutation," and having circumambulated the Goddess, saying "Salute her," [he salutes] with both hands.

Touching the ears: "I am of the Kāśyapa, Āvatsāra, and Naiddhrava lineages; all these being the *pravara* lineages of the Kāśyapa *gotra*. I am a student of the Bodhāyana-sūtra, a reciter of the Yajur-veda branch, and my name is So-and-so Śarman, sir. (L2. Having said this, he should slowly wipe [the body] with both hands from the two knees down to the big toes of the feet. Then: "Homage to the eastern direction! Homage to the southern direction! Homage to the western direction! Homage to the northern direction! Homage to the upward direction! Homage to the downward direction! Homage to the intermediate space!"

"Salutation to the direction; salutation to the direction of the earth"— having thus performed a circumambulation of the directions clockwise, he faces the south and [offers oblations] to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka,
Vaivasvata, Kāla, and Sarvabhūtakṣaya.
Salutations to Audumbara, Dadhnya, Nīla, and Parameṣṭhin;
salutations indeed to Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta. Salutations again and again to Śrī Citragupta. [Facing] westward...
O Govinda, O lotus-eyed one, protect me who have come to you for refuge— you who possess the conch, discus, and mace, and whose chariot is drawn by the horses Śaibya and Sugrīva.

Facing north, [he meditates upon] the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose semen is drawn up, and who has diverse eyes—to the one of universal form, salutation! To the illustrious Viśvarūpa, indeed, salutation after salutation! Facing east: salutation to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world, the cause of the world’s origin, maintenance, and destruction; to the one consisting of the three Vedas, the sustainer of the nature of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), [the essence of] the *ajapā-gāyatrī*.
To Śaṅkara, who is the self of Viriñci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara; just as water fallen from the sky goes to the ocean, so does the salutation of all the gods go toward Śaṅkara.

Departing toward Śrī Śaṅkara, [one says] "Obeisance. Having recollected all the deities, beginning with mother, father, and guru, and having offered salutation and risen, one should again offer obeisance twelve times to the Sun. Then, [one should confess]: "Whatever transgression has been committed by hand or foot, or born of speech, body, hearing, sight, or mind; whether prescribed or unprescribed—all this, O Śiva, Śiva, O ocean of compassion, O Śrī Mahādeva Śambhu, forgive!

Now, being capable, prior to the commencement of the *gāyatrī* recitation, one should perform the recitation of the *ajapā-gāyatrī*, as well as the internal (*antarmātṛkā*) and external (*bahirmātṛkā*) *nyāsa* rituals.

Having performed [these preliminaries], one should thereafter begin the recitation (*japa*) of the *gāyatrī*. It is as follows: "Beginning today from sunrise until the next sunrise, I shall perform the recitation of twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations of the *ajapā-gāyatrī* mantra in the form of inhalation and exhalation. Of this venerable *gāyatrī* mantra named *ajapā*, Haṃsa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the unmanifest *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandas*), Paramahaṃsa is the deity (*devatā*), Haṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Saṃ is the power (*śakti*), and So'haṃ is the pin (*kīlaka*). [This is for] the purpose of attaining the grace of Paramahaṃsa and for the sake of liberation."

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation of the *Ajapā Gāyatrī* mantra: *Haṃ sāṃ* to the Sun-self, salutation to both thumbs; *Haṃ siṃ* to the Moon-self, to the index fingers; *Haṃ sūṃ* to the Stainless-self (*nirañjana*), to the middle fingers; *Haṃ saiṃ* to the Effulgence-less-self (*nirābhāsa*), to the ring fingers; *Haṃ sauṃ* to the Bodyless, Embodied, Subtle-self, salutation to both little fingers; *Haṃ saṃ* to the Unmanifest-self (*avyakta*), to the palms. Thus is the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). [The placement on the joints (*sandhi*) follows. The visualization (*dhyāna*): [... [text fragment] [... [text fragment].

The Swan, who pervades the universe, possesses the two syllables *agni* and *soma*, the *praṇava*, and the *bindu*; he is radiant with three eyes, has a face as brilliant as Rudra, and his pair of feet are Śiva’s; by his sides stand Sūrya and Agni, and he resembles many millions of rising suns.
One should always meditate upon that which consists of Brahman within the nest of the lotus-palace of the heart.
O auspicious one, born from the mouth of the *mūlādhāra*, embraced by flames,
with the rite of consecration performed by the nectar of the lunar orb suspended above;
[you who are] filled with the nectar of bliss through the perceptions and observations of the objects of the senses via the channels (*nāḍī*).
The deity whose nature is sound resides within the pavilion.
In the *āvāra* [the base], at the navel, in the heart-lotus, at the root of the palate, and on the forehead;
in the two petals, the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the twenty-petaled, the twelve-petaled, and the four-petaled;
at the end of the abode, in the center of the *bāla*, together with *ḍa*, *pha*, *ka*, *ṭha*, *sa*, and *ha*; and at the end of the consonants (*halānta*)—therein reside *aṃ* and the *visarga*.
I bow to that which is the middle *haṃsa*, well-illuminated, endowed with all its digits (*kalās*), and whose form is the primordial syllable (*varṇa*).
The foundation (ādhāra) has four petals and is reddish-brown in color;
the svādhiṣṭhāna is like many flashes of lightning and has six petals ending with the letter *ba*;
the maṇipūraka is red in appearance and has ten petals, beginning with the letter *ḍa* and ending with the letter *pha*.
With twelve petals, the golden city of Anāhata is surrounded by the Kaṭha syllables at its extremities.
The city of Ājñā is a pure lotus of light, joined with the sixteen vowels as its petals,
possessing the two syllable-seeds totaling two hundred thousand [recitations], and having a reddish hue.
Above that is an upward-facing, blossomed lotus with a thousand petals.
I am indeed capable of bowing to Sadāśiva, who is eternal bliss and everlasting.
In the pavilion of the *mūlādhāra*, salutation to Śakti-Gaṇapati, who resides in the center of the pericarp of the four-petalled lotus: "I choose you,
the lord of the hosts (*gaṇādhyakṣa*), girt with a serpent as a sacred thread."
One should meditate upon the god Gaṇanātha, who holds a noose and a goad.

Having meditated thus: *Namaḥ* to Gaṇanātha. *Laṃ*, to the self of Earth, I offer fragrance. *Gaṇa*, *Ha*, to the self of Space, flowers. *Gaṇa*, *Yaṃ*, to the self of Wind, incense. *Gaṇā*, *Raṃ*, to the self of Fire, a lamp. *Gaṇa*, *Vaṃ*, to the self of Nectar, the nectar-offering (*amṛta-naivedya*). Having worshipped with these five offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using their respective mudrās, I offer day and night the recitation of six hundred repetitions of the name-gāyatrī mantra to Gaṇanātha: *Vaṃ namaḥ*, *Śaṃ namaḥ*, *Ṣaṃ namaḥ*, *Saṃ namaḥ*. Oṃ.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) four times on the four-petaled lotus with the mantra "I am that *haṃsa*," and having recited once: "We know the *haṃsa*, the female *haṃsī*; we meditate upon him as *haṃsa*; may that *haṃsa* [who is] I impel me. Then, in the pavilion of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, in the center of the pericarp of the six-petaled lotus, one should pay homage to Brahmā: "Obeisance to Brahmā. One should contemplate Brahmā, the eternal Sun, who holds a staff and a water-pot, whose form is the letter *A*, and who is the very embodiment of Brahman. "Obeisance to Brahmā. Having worshipped him as before, [one proceeds with] the enclosure...
I offer this recitation of mantras day and night, consisting of the six-syllable [mantra] and the name-mantra. *Namaḥ*. On the three petals: *Haṃsaḥ so 'ham* three times. Again, on the three petals:

*Yaṃ namaḥ*, *Raṃ namaḥ*, *Laṃ namaḥ*; and *Haṃsaḥ so 'ham* three times. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) in sequence upon the six petals, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra once. Then, in the pavilion of the *Maṇipūraka*, in the center of the pericarp of the ten-petaled lotus: *Viṣṇave namaḥ*.
One should contemplate the god Viṣṇu, the infallible one, who bears the conch and the discus and is clothed in yellow garments,
in the form of the syllable *ukāra*.

Having performed worship for Viṣṇu as before: "I offer up six thousand ajapā recitations of the Gāyatrī mantra to Viṣṇu, day and night. Having placed [the syllables] upon the ten petals—*ḍaṃ namaḥ*, *haṃsaḥ so'haṃ* (l4), *ḍhaṃ*, *haṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, *haṃ*, *taṃ*, *haṃ*, *thaṃ*, *haṃ*, *daṃ*, *haṃ*, *dhaṃ*, *haṃ*, *naṃ*, *haṃ*, *paṃ*, *haṃ*, *phaṃ*, *namaḥ*, *haṃsaḥ so'ham*—one should then recite the Haṃsa-Gāyatrī once. Then, in the Anāhata pavilion, to Rudra situated in the center of the pericarp of the twelve-petaled lotus: *namaḥ*. [He is] holding a trident and a drum in his hands, and possessing a rosary and a skull-bowl.

One should contemplate the form of Rudra in the form of the syllable *m*. "Salutation to Rudra. Having performed the worship as before, one offers the recitation of the *Ajapā-Gāyatrī* mantra six thousand times for Rudra: *kaṃ namaḥ*, *haṃ saḥ ahaṃ*, *khaṃ haṃ*, *gaṃ haṃ*, *yaṃ haṃ*, *ṅaṃ haṃ*, *caṃ haṃ*, *chaṃ haṃ*, *jaṃ haṃ*, *jhaṃ haṃ*, *ñaṃ haṃ*, *ṭaṃ haṃ*, *ṭhaṃ haṃ*, *ssaḥ ahaṃ*. Having thus assigned [these] to the twelve petals, one should recite the *Haṃsa-Gāyatrī* once; thereafter, [one offers it] to him who resides in the center of the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus in the Viśuddhi pavilion.
Salutation to the individual self (jīvātman).
One should contemplate the form of the living soul, resembling pure crystal, possessing a luster equal to the light of the moon, situated in the middle of the path of the Suṣumṇā.

Salutation to the Jīvātman. Having performed the worship as before: "I offer one thousand recitations of the Ajapā-Gāyatrī mantra to the Jīvātman. Having uttered "Aṃ Āṃ Iṃ Īṃ Uṃ Ūṃ Ṛṃ Ṝṃ Namaḥ Haṃsaḥ So'ham" eight times, and again having recited "Ḷṃ Ḹṃ Eṃ Aiṃ Oṃ Auṃ Aṃ Āḥ Namaḥ Haṃsaḥ So'ham" eight times, and having thus assigned [the mantras] to the sixteen petals in this sequence, one should recite the Haṃsa-Gāyatrī once. Thereafter, to the form of the venerable Guru situated in the center of the pericarp of the lotus of petals in the Pavilion of the Command (Ājñā-maṇṭapa):

Homage! One should contemplate the form of the Guru, who is like the sun for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, situated within the circle of the sky. Homage to the form of the Guru! Having performed worship as before, one should place the *ajāpā-gāyatrī* [mantra] "So 'haṃ, So 'haṃ" a thousand times upon the two petals of the Guru. Then, one should recite the *haṃsa-gāyatrī* once.
Homage to the Supreme Self, who dwells in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus within the pavilion of Brahman. Homage!
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, who is truth, eternal, supreme knowledge, absolute, and whose nature is pure consciousness, resembling ten million suns in brilliance.

Salutation to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Having performed the worship as before, I offer one thousand recitations of the *ajāpā-gāyatrī* mantra of the Supreme Self: *Aṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ aṃ namaḥ | Laṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ laṃ namaḥ | Aṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ aṃ namaḥ.* Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) along with its limbs (*aṅga*) according to the sequence of ascent and descent, once again: *Aṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ aṃ namaḥ | Laṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ laṃ namaḥ | Laṃ namaḥ haṃsassohaṃ laṃ namaḥ | Aṃ namaḥ.*

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the head eighteen times, moving clockwise and counter-clockwise, by ascending and descending through the sequence of syllables beginning with *haṃ* and ending with *so'haṃ namaḥ*; having recited the *Haṃsa-gāyatrī*, "Yo'sau so'haṃ," once; and having displayed the *Nirvāṇa-mudrā*, [one should recite] the *Ajapā-gāyatrī*: "We know the Stainless One (*nirañjana*), we meditate upon the Effulgence-less One (*nirābhāsa*), may He, who is not subtle yet subtle, impel us. Thus [ends the section on] the internal and external *mātṛkā-nyāsa*.

l1. One should recite thus; having performed the internal placement (*antar-mātṛkā-nyāsa*) preceded by the recitation of the *ajāpā* mantra, one should perform the external placement (*bahir-mātṛkā-nyāsa*). For this venerable *sabindu-bahirmātṛkā-sarasvatī* mantra, Śabdabrahman is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Devīgāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Sabindumātrikāsarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*).
