Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhavasvadhā; on the right arm. Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Udbhava, salutation to Dhṛti; on the left arm. Of this great mantra of the Śrī Pañcākṣara-nyāsa: Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi); Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ); Sāmbasadāśiva is the deity (devatā); Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Namaḥ is the power (śakti).
The *kīlaka* is for Śiva. The application (*viniyoga*) is in the ritual placement of my own body.
[Now, the placement of the five-syllable mantra (*pañcākṣaranyāsa*):

*(Oṃ namaḥ)* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*). *Oṃ namaḥ* on the head (*śiras*). *Naṃ namaḥ* on the face (*mukha*). *Maṃ namaḥ* on the heart (*hṛdaya*). *Śiṃ namaḥ* on the private parts (*guhya*). *Vaṃ namaḥ* on the feet (*pāda*). *Yaṃ namaḥ* on the feet (*pāda*).

Now follows the Śrīkaṇṭha-Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Of this great mantra of the Śrī Śrīkaṇṭha-Mātṛkā-nyāsa, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi); Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda); Sarasvatī, whose essence is the syllables, is the deity; *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *svaḥ* is the power (*śakti*). My application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of liberation through the ritual placement upon the body. *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīm aṃ*, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī—on the head. *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ*, salutation to Ananta and Vijayā—on the perimeter of the mouth. *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīm iṃ*... on the forehead. (Line 5)

Salutation to Sūkṣma and Śālinī; [this is] for the right eye (in this sequence). The seed-syllable is *Īṃ* everywhere: salutation to Trimūrti and Lolākṣī; [this is] for the left eye. *Uṃ*: salutation to Amareśvara and Vartulā; [this is] for the right ear. *Ūṃ*: salutation to Arpiśa and Dīrghakoṇā; [this is] for the left ear. *Ṛṃ*: salutation to Bhārabhūti and Dīrghamukhī; [this is] for the right nostril-passage (*puṭa*). *Ṛṃ*: salutation to Nidhaneśa and Gomukhī; [this is] for the left nostril-passage. *Ḷṃ*: salutation to Sthāṇu and Dīrghajihvā.

On the right cheek: *ḷṃ* to Harakuṇḍodarī; on the left cheek: *eṃ* [to] Ūrdhvakeśī, obeisance. On the upper lip: *aiṃ* to Bhautika and Akṛta; on the lower lip: *oṃ* to Sadyojāta and Jvālāmukhī. On the upper row of teeth: *aum* to Anugraheśa and Ulkāmukhī; on the lower row of teeth: *am* to Akrūra and Śrīmukhī. On the crown of the head: [to] Mahāsena and Vidyā. On the mouth: *kaṃ* to Krodheśa and Mahākālī; on the right arm: *khaṃ* to Caṇḍeśa and Sarasvatī.

(…) *So* and *Śakhecarī* at the base of the right thigh; *Ṭhaṃ* and *Lāṅgalimañjarī* at the right knee; *Ḍaṃ* and *Dārukarūpiṇī* at the tip of the right shank; *Ḍhaṃ* and *Ardhanārīśavikariṇī* at the right foot; *Ṇaṃ* and *Umākānta* (…) at the toes of the right foot; *Taṃ* and *Āṣāḍhapūtanā* at the base of the left thigh; *Thaṃ* and *Muṇḍibhadrakālī* at the left knee; *Daṃ* and *Atrigomatī* at the tip of the left shank; *Dhaṃ* and *Īśānaśaṅkhinī* at the left foot; *Naṃ*...

*Me* and *Ṣa* are on the toes of the left foot with Meṣagarjanī; *Pa* on the right [toes] with Lohitākālarātri; *Pha* on the left side with Śikhikubjanī; *Ba* on the back with Chagalaraṇḍakamanī; *Bha* at the navel with Dviraṇḍavajraṇī; *Ma* at the belly with Mahākālajayā; *Ya* at the heart with Sumukheśvarī; *Ra* at the base of the right arm with Bhuja...vatī; *La* at the base of the left arm with Pinākimādhavī; *Va* at the back of the neck with Khaḍgīravārumī; *Śa* at the right armpit with Bakayādhavī.

*Ṣaṃ* to Śveta and Rakṣopasāriṇī on the left armpit; *saṃ* to Mṛga and Sahajā on the right foot; *haṃ* to Lakulīśa and Lakṣmī on the left foot; *ḷaṃ* salutation to Rūpa and Vyāpinī; *kṣaṃ* salutation to Saṃvartaka and Āminī—from the mouth to the belly. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, one should then perform the internal worship (*antar-pūjā*). Salutation to the Self (*ātman*); salutation to the Inner Self (*antarātman*); salutation to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); salutation to the Self of Knowledge (*jñānātman*); salutation to the embodiment of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda-mūrti*). Having thus worshipped within oneself, [one says]: *laṃ* salutation to Śiva.

I offer fragrance with the earth-nature to Sāmbasadāśiva. Haṃ Namaḥ … [with the] soul-nature … [I offer] a flower. Yaṃ Namaḥ … [with the] air-nature … I offer incense. Mi … I offer. Raṃ Namaḥ … [with the] fire-nature … [I offer] a lamp. Vaṃ Namaḥ … [with the] nectar-nature … Sāṃ … I offer the nectar-food offering. Having thus worshipped, or alternatively: (line 2).
I worship my own *liṅga*, which resembles a jewel,
situated within the lotus of the heart-city of *māyā*,
through the consecrations of the pure water of the mind from the river of faith.
Constantly [worship] with the flowers of meditative concentration for the sake of non-rebirth. ||1||
A seat fashioned of jewels, a bath with snowy waters, and divine garments;
ornaments of various gems, sandalwood enhanced by the fragrance of musk;
flowers born of the *jātī*, *campaka*, *mallikā*, and *vakula* trees, as well as incense.
O Lord, O ocean of divine compassion, accept this lamp for your satisfaction.

(2) [L4] Having placed upon a supreme golden vessel inlaid with clusters of jewels various foods—well-cooked solid foods (*bhakṣya*), soft foods (*bhojya*), lickable foods (*lehya*) endowed with manifold flavors, and food to be sucked (*coṣya*)—along with the scent of cow-products... [text continues].
Every day, I mentally offer to you my own self as a vessel filled with various vegetables, ghee, honey, curd, milk, and meat, along with betel-leaf prepared according to your own nature. ||3||

The parasol, the pair of chowries, the fan, the ten musical instruments— maddala, bherī, śaṅkha, mṛdaṅga, kāhala, sweet song, and likewise dance— as well as the prostration with eight limbs and various other offerings: all of this has been performed by me.
O All-pervading Lord, may that which is offered by my resolve be conducive to Your excellence. ||4||
You are the Self; the mind of the Daughter of the Mountain is your retinue; the vital breaths are your servants; the body is your home;
the arrangement of the enjoyment of sense objects is your worship; sleep is your state of meditative absorption (samādhi);
the movement of the two feet is the rite of circumambulation; and all [actions] are your hymns of praise.
Whatever action I perform, O Śambhu, all of that is your worship. ||5||

Having performed the mental worship (*mānasī-pūjā*) as described in these five verses and having meditated upon oneself as being of the nature of Śiva, one should then form the resolve: "I shall now perform the external worship. Having recited the five-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times, one should perform the worship of the water-jar (*kalaśa*). Having worshipped Indra and the other deities in the four directions of the jar, one should worship with scents and other offerings in the center, saying: "Obeisance to Brahmā. At the mouth [of the jar], saying: "Obeisance to Rudra. At the neck, saying: "Obeisance to Viṣṇu. At the base, saying: "Obeisance to Brahmā. In the middle, [saying]: "To the hosts of Mothers."

Homage! Homage to the oceans within the womb [of the earth]. Homage to the Earth, possessed of the seven continents. Homage to the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas along with their ancillaries. May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, and lakes come to the sacrifice of the patron, effecting the destruction of his misfortunes.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Godāvarī, and the Sarasvatī.

Having recited the mantra: "I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one; many kindle this [Agni] who belongs to the five peoples.

Having entered into every clan, O Lord of Wealth, release us from that [bond]. Then, having poured a little water from the conch into the pitcher with the Gāyatrī mantra, and having taken a little water in his hand, he should mutter the root mantra eight times and sprinkle the articles of worship and himself.

Having filled five vessels with water using the root mantra alone: the general *arghya* vessel in the eastern part of the conch; the *ācamanīya* vessel to the west of the conch; the *arghya* vessel to the west of the *ācamanīya*;

O Lord, I prepare this *madhuparka*; be gracious to me. *Triyam* [obeisance]. I offer the *madhuparka*. Of this great mantra of the *Śrī Rudrapraśna*, Aghora is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), and that Sun who is the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) in the form of the *Saṃkarṣaṇa-mūrti* is the deity (*devatā*). *Namaśśivāya* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Śivatarāya* is the power (*śakti*). *Sadāśivāya* is the pin (*kīlaka*). For the sake of my enjoyment and liberation, and for the pleasure of Sāmbasadāśiva...

The application (*viniyoga*) for the consecration of Śiva: Salutation to the Self of the Agnihotra with both thumbs; Salutation to the Self of the Darśapūrṇamāsa with the two index fingers; Salutation to the Self of the Cāturmāsya with [the two middle fingers]; Salutation to the Self of the Paśubandha with [the two ring fingers]; Salutation to the Self of the Agniṣṭoma with [the two little fingers]; Salutation to the Self who has performed [the sacrifice] four million times with [the heart]. Thus is the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*—this is the bond (*bandha*).
His meditation causes the entire cosmic egg— the world from the depths of the netherworld to the vault of the sky—
to tremble; and by the nectars flowing from the full moon shimmering upon the crest of his crystal liṅga of light, [he bestows immortality].

For the sake of attaining one's desired goal, a Brahmin should incessantly recite the *Rudrādhyāya* with rapid cadence while meditating on the one Lord who is not submerged in the slightest [worldly state]; he should then consecrate Śiva.
*oṃ śaṃ ca me śāntiḥ | oṃ namas te rudra manyava uta īṣave namas te | taṃ vo jaṃbhe dadhāmi | tryambakaṃ yajāmahe | yo rudro...*

Let it be so. Praise him, the one who perceives. Om, Agni and Viṣṇu, and the Lord. Peace. The peace-chant three times and five times. (I shall perform) the bath along with its primary and secondary limbs very gradually. "To the Three-Eyed One, salutation!"—this is the bath. Having offered the water for rinsing the mouth as a limb of the bath as before, having sprinkled [the deity] with the *vyāhṛtis*, and having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the eight names beginning with "I satiate the god Bhava," then, having wiped [him] dry with a fine cloth and established him upon a lion-throne, one should offer a flower with the mantra: "Salutation to Sthāṇu, to Śambhu. [This is] the garment of knowledge and protection for his own secret splendor, which was previously covered by the variegated cloth of *māyā*.

I offer these to You. This garment: to that Supreme Lord, depending upon whom the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who eternally deludes the world, exists—to Him I offer this upper garment. *Tryaṃ*... this upper garment. As before, the water for sipping (ācamana). To Him whose power by means of the triad has completely pervaded this entire universe—to that [Lord], one should offer the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*). *Tryaṃ*... obeisance. Thus, the sacrificial thread is offered to Him whose limbs are beautiful by nature and who rests upon various powers. Various ornaments.

I fashion this ornament, worshipped by the immortals. O Supreme Lord, out of compassion, please accept this supreme fragrance that fills the quarters of space with the perfume of supreme bliss; I offer this fragrance, which is the gateway to prosperity. This fourth garment is composed of various qualities and is enchanting; let this excellent flower, whose fragrance is bliss, be accepted. *Tryambaka*, obeisance. [Offer] the flower. Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra (*mūla*) and having adorned [the deity] with garlands of flowers and so forth, [one should worship] with the root mantra.

Having worshipped with *bilva* leaves and other varieties of flowers, [one should offer incense with the mantra: "Endowed with the essence of the trees, rich in fragrance, this supreme scent—this incense, which is to be smelled by all beings, may it be accepted. (*dhūr asi*, *masi*, *tryaṃ dhūpam*). [One should offer the lamp with the mantra: "O great lamp, well-illuminated, dispelling darkness on all sides, this lamp, the light for both the exterior and the interior, may it be accepted. (*uddīpyasva*, *daya*, *tryaṃ dīpam*). Then, from the Sun onwards, up to one's chosen deity, having invoked those serpents with their respective mantras, [one should worship them] with the preliminary offerings (*upacāras*).

Having performed worship and placed [the offerings] all around Śiva, then [regarding] the *naivedya*: having set aside a portion for the *vaiśvadeva* and placed it elsewhere, one should lift up a vessel of food containing ghee and side-dishes for the purpose of offering to Śiva. Having divided [the remainder] separately for the retinue and placed it in [other] vessels, one should offer it beginning with Śiva. Having consecrated the food with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *Śivagāyatrī*, and having sprinkled water with the mantra "Satyaṃ tvartena," one should pour water for the deity with the mantra "Amṛtopastaraṇam asi. Then, having recited the mantra for the *prāṇāhuti* offerings, thus...

Having recited these mantras—"I am [offering] separately," "The winds blow honey," "By the impulse of the God," "He says to the rice-porridge," and "May I become abundant"—one should offer that which is endowed with the six kinds of food and the six flavors, accompanied by side dishes and drenched in clarified butter, saying: "O Lord of Gods, I present this; accept it together with your attendants. Then, one offers the Great Offering (*mahānivedya*) with the mantra "Tryambakaṃ... and the mantra "Thou art the vessel for the drinking of nectar. Having offered water, one says: "O Lord of the gods of all gods, [this offering] which brings satisfaction to all."

"O you who are filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water; accept three mouthfuls for rinsing and sipping, and this water for drinking. Accept this betel nut together with its accompaniments—three times.

[Accept] the betel leaf. Having given the water for sipping: 'May Bāṇa, Rāvaṇa, Caṇḍeśa, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Vṛṣa, and the others—all these followers of Śambhu—accept this offering from the Supreme Lord. Thus, having given the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) to Caṇḍeśa and the others, then [offer] incense, lamps, ornaments, camphor lamps, and sacred ash."

Having offered [the oblation] with the bases of the umbrella, palm-leaf fan, whisk, chowrie, mirror, and so forth; having worshipped with the *mantra-puṣpa* [offering] using the mantra: "O Agni, you are Rudra, always our... and so on; having worshipped Bhava... and so on; having worshipped with eight hundred and eight or one thousand and eight bilva leaves or excellent flowers, using the eight names beginning with Bhava; having worshipped the eight [deities] beginning with Brahmā in the locations starting from the east; and having again recited the five-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of destroying great sins and for the attainment of the supreme boon, [one should perform] circumambulation.
"I act [thus], O Lord; be gracious, O Supreme Lord. Having thus performed three circumambulations:
"Salutations to you, Somanātha, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, and who has made the crescent moon his crest-ornament."
O Śaṅkara, bestower of enjoyment and liberation, and remover of all sins, do not consider me a mere servant; destroy my sin!

"Salutation be to Śambhu. Having offered a flower: "Salutation to Śiva, together with Ambā, the cause of the three causes; I offer myself to you, O Supreme Lord—you are my refuge. Having thus performed the self-satiation (*ātmatarpaṇa*).
Whatever action has been performed by me, whether virtuous or non-virtuous,
may all that, O Blessed One Śambhu, become supreme worship of you.
Fulfill [this] here; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
I do not know the invocation, nor do I know that [rite of] dismissal.
I do not know the ritual of worship, nor the mantra, nor the procedure;
I do not even know your true nature—forgive me, O ocean of compassion!
Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ oṃ. I bid farewell to Śiva.
O Śaṅkara, having entered the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus together with Ambā, [remain] within the great [abode], free from all veils.

Thus, having dismissed Sāmbaśiva residing in the *liṅga* into the lotus of the heart, one should then rotate a water-filled conch shell over the three-eyed Lord. The water situated within the conch, having been rotated over Śaṅkara, would burn away even the sin of killing a Brahmin committed by men for as many years as there are drops. Thus it is said.

Having sprinkled water on one's head and taken the sacred water (tīrtha) with the mantra "Ṛtaṃ satyam," and having drunk the water from the remains of the offering (nirmālya) of the trident-bearing God of gods,
one is liberated from consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and other such afflictions, as well as from sins. (Vaiśvadeva)
The auspicious water from the feet of Śiva and Ambā wards off untimely death, destroys all diseases,
and effects the destruction of all sins.

One should lead [the fire] to its proper place. One should perform the Vaiśvadeva oblation either at the *aupāsana* or the *pacana* fire. Having leveled the ground in a clean and even spot and having established the fire, one should strew grass around it. [Saying: "I shall perform the *śakala-homa* for the removal of sin," one sprinkles water around the fire from left to right. Having sprinkled the wood-shavings (*śakala*), he offers them: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā!"

The expiation for what has been done by oneself... you are the means of its removal; *svāhā*. The expiation for whatever sin we have committed by day or by night, you are the means of its removal; *svāhā*. The expiation for whatever sin we have committed, whether knowingly or unknowingly, you are the means of its removal; *svāhā*. The expiation for this sin... you are the means of its removal; *svāhā*. Protect us for Agni... *svāhā*. Protect us for... knowledge; *svāhā*. Protect the sacrifice, O Radiant One; *svāhā*. Protect everything, O Lord of a Hundred Powers; *svāhā*. Protect us, O Agni, with your first [power]; protect us also with your second; protect us... *svāhā*.

With three verses, [saying] "O Lord of Strengths, protect... [and] "O Vasu, svāhā!"—[reciting] "bhūḥ svāhā, bhuvaḥ svāhā, suvaḥ svāhā," and "oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā"—thus seventeen [times]. [This is the rule of] Hārita. Having set aside [the portion] for the Vaiśvadeva, one should offer it to the deity facing east. Then, having performed the Vaiśvadeva according to the rules for the *ātma-karman*, one should then perform breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and sprinkle water around the fire. Then, [thinking] "I shall perform the Vaiśvadeva oblation": "To Agni, svāhā! To Agni, svāhā! To Soma..."

Svāhā! To Dhruva; to Dhruva Bhauma; to Dhruvakṣiti; to Acyutakṣiti, svāhā! To Īśāna, svāhā! To Jayanta, svāhā! To Dharmaruci; to Dhanvantari; to Sva-vidyā; to Ambikā; to Hari; to the Sthāvira Gaṇas, svāhā! To the Gaṇapatīs, svāhā! To the Assemblies; to the Viśvedevas; to the Sādhyas; to all the gods, svāhā! Bhūr svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Suvaḥ svāhā!

*Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ svāhā-hā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā!*—with these words, he offers [the oblation] in the eastern half of the northern half [of the fire]. Behind the fire, he presents the *bali* offering on the ground, ending toward the east. Having restrained his breath, he says: "I shall perform the *baliharaṇa*. *To Dharma, svāhā! To Adharma, svāhā!* [He offers] in front of the fire. *To Kadru... [one cubit] deep, svāhā! To all, svāhā!* Having sprinkled water around [the fire], if he is unable to perform [the offerings] at the hearth and other such places, he should offer the *balis* in eight rows to the north of the fire, ending toward the north, with each row directed toward the east.

(l5. To the goddess Acalā, svāhā! To Vāstupālī with her retinue, svāhā! To these [goddesses], svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Prajāpati, to Parameṣṭhin, to Ṛṣabha, to Rudra, to Rudrāṇī, svāhā! Having sprinkled around, there is one row of nine: (p44a., f41b., l1. To the plants and trees, svāhā! To the Rakṣas and the divine folk, svāhā! To Kāma, to Bhaga, to Śrī, to Viṣṇu, to (…)hāya, to (…)harāja, svāhā! Having sprinkled around, there is one row of eight: (2)

Alternatively, 22) … *svāhā* to wealth and grain; *svāhā* to Vaiśravaṇa; to Śrī; to Puṣṭi; to the mortar and pestle; to the upper and lower millstones; to the goddess Samūhinī. Having sprinkled [water] around, [there is] the *saptadaśa-paṅkti*. Alternatively, 23) *svāhā* to the household deities (*gṛhyāḥ*); to the resting places; to the lords of the resting places; to all the divine folk; *svāhā* to all beings. *Svāhā* to the intermediate space; to the one who dwells in the intermediate space; to Dhātṛ; to Vidhātṛ, *svāhā*. Having sprinkled [water] around...

A single row with nine [offerings]. 4. *Svāhā* to prosperity (*bhūti*), to abundance (*prabhūti*). That which moves in the world, that which stirs, the portion of the Name belonging to the Name—*svāhā*.

To the two elders (*jyeṣṭha*). To the two hands (*karaskara*). To Śrī. To Viṣṇu. To Rudra, to cattle, to Paśupati—*svāhā*. Having sprinkled around, a single row with ten [offerings]. 5. *Svāhā* to Vāstoṣpati. To the earth, to the intermediate space, to the sky—*svāhā*. To Sūrya. To Candramas. To the constellations (*nakṣatra*). To the waters. To the plants.

Having sprinkled [the water] for the trees (*vanaspati*), there is one row of twelve [offerings]. 6. For the moving and unmoving beings (*carācara*), for the floating beings (*pariplava*), for the crawling beings (*sarisṛpa*), for the regions (*deśa*), for the times (*kāla*), for the worlds (*loka*), for the Vedas (*veda*), and having sprinkled for the seers (*ṛṣi*)... thus there is one row of eight [offerings]. For the Vasus, for the Rudras, for the Ādityas, for Indra, for Bṛhaspati, for Prajāpati, for Brahman *svāhā*. Having sprinkled, there is one row of seven [offerings]. 8. Altogether, there are sixty [offerings]. To the south.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīti): "To the grandfathers, svadhā! Homage! Svāhā! To the great-grandfathers, svāhā! Having touched water and having sprinkled around [the offering], wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), to the north: "Homage to Rudra, the Blessed One, svāhā! Then, having touched water, in the directions starting from the east: "To the eastern direction, svāhā! To the northern direction, svāhā! To the western direction, svāhā! To the southern direction, svāhā! In the center: "To the upward direction; to the downward direction. In the intermediate directions: "To Yama; to Nirṛti."

*svāhā* to the Rākṣasas; *svāhā* to Īśāna. Having touched water, he should sprinkle it into the air: "To those beings who roam by day and by night, seeking strength and acting as the messengers of Vituda—to them I offer this oblation, desiring prosperity. May the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me, *svāhā*. [He pours] the rinsing of the vessel toward the north-eastern direction: "Homage to Rudra, the earthly one, *svāhā*. Having touched water, he should then perform the fifth sacrifice: "I shall perform the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). "You are lightning (*vidyut*)."

Having touched water, having sprinkled around [the fire] with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he offers an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to the gods. Having touched water, having sprinkled around the fire, and having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he stands up. Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he says: "I shall perform the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). Having touched water and sprinkled [around the fire], he pours out water to the south of the fire with "Svadhā and obeisance to the ancestors. And [he offers] into the fire with "Svadhā and obeisance to the ancestors, svāhā."

He should offer oblations. Having sprinkled [water] around with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ," he then, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (upavītī), says: "I shall perform the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña). Having touched water and sprinkled [around], he should offer in the fire to the west of it with "bhūtebhyaḥ svāhā. May rain come! Having sprinkled [around], he says: "I shall perform the sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña). Having touched water and sprinkled [around], he should divide the food with "manuṣyebhyaḥ ahaṃ na" (for men, I [offer] not) and then offer in the fire with "manuṣyebhyaḥ svāhā. May rain come!

Having sprinkled [water] around, one should say, "I shall perform the *brahmayajña*. Having sprinkled [water] again, one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra, "To Brahman, svāhā! and [the mantra], "You are rain... and "Go to the earth. Then, having sprinkled [water] around, one should offer the *bali* for dogs and crows. Having gone outside, the *bali* for dogs: "The two dogs, Śyāma and Śabala, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata—to them I shall give this rice-ball; may they be my protectors against evil. The *bali* for crows: "May those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Yama, and Nirṛti accept these milk-rice offerings."

A *puṇḍra* has been offered by me upon the ground; this is the universal offering (*sarvabali*). Gods, humans, cattle, birds, perfected beings (*siddhas*), hosts of *yakṣas*, serpents, and spirits, as well as *pretas*, trees, and all others who desire food—may they receive what is given by me. Having performed the *vaiśvadeva* oblations, I desire the satisfaction [of these beings]. At the time of milking the cow, one should set aside the first portion and give it [to them]. Then, having sat down behind the *gārhapatya* fire, or behind the *aupāsana* fire, seated upon *darbha* grass and holding *darbha* blades, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having recited the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or ten times; having recited the Saṃhitā-anuvāka beginning with "The Vedas, the four fires, the head of heaven, the peak," and the Acchidra-anuvāka beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods"; and having concluded with the mantra "Obeisance to Brahman" repeated three times along with the Praṇava (Om), he should then offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). He should sacrifice: *svāhā* to the desired; *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā* to the undesired; *svāhā* to the remedy for ill-omened offerings; *svāhā* to Hārītakī; *svāhā* to misfortune; and *svāhā* to the divine bodies.

" Svāhā! To success, svāhā! To complete success, svāhā! To all-round success, svāhā! Thus he offers for the success of the sacrifice. In the absence of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should offer with barley and other grains. The sacrifice is of two kinds: first, the *brahmayajña* and others such as the recitation of the *praśna* [texts]; the *devayajña* consists of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation and others; the *pitṛyajña* consists of the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth performed with a sense of rivalry [or distinction];
the *bhūtayajña* is the offering of bali; and the *manuṣyayajña* is the honoring of guests. Furthermore, there is another set of five sacrifices prescribed by Dharma following the bali-offering.

The *brahmayajña*—consisting of the *devayajña* and other rites—should be performed either before or after the libation (*tarpaṇa*), or following the morning oblation (*prātarāhuti*). It may also be performed at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* rite on account of specific occasions; thus it is done at all three times of day. Alternatively, the performance of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) at a time subsequent to the midday *sandhyā* worship is more authoritative. One should offer the sacrificial portions (*balis*) in their respective places according to the method taught by the Teacher.

If one is unable to do so physically, one should perform them mentally, arranging them in eight rows to the north of the fire, or else in the form of an anthill. [The five types of offerings are: burning, cooking, cutting, bending, and...

Regarding the grinding [of grain]: "The five slaughterhouses are the expiation," so say those most learned in the single scripture (*eka-śāstra*). But the Teacher says: "By the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the twice-born attain divinity; by the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), they attain the state of ancestors; by the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), they become beings; by the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*), they become men; and by the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), one becomes a Brāhmaṇa. Having attained equality with these deities for a hundred years, they go to the bliss of Brahman—firm, eternal, and imperishable. If a religious student (*brahmacārin*) arrives for alms, one should address him kindly and give him a bowl (*kapāla*).

One should give alms. Now, having invited the ascetic who has arrived, saying "Welcome," and having paid homage, performed the washing of his feet and other rites, one should feed him as much as required.

Upon seeing a guest arrive, one should rise, address him with kind words, provide a seat and so forth, and serve him by offering food. In the absence of food, one should at least offer a seat; even the offering of water for the feet is auspicious. In this manner, one should honor all who have come, down to the outcaste (caṇḍāla). If a mendicant arrives before the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been performed, [one should offer him food].

Having set aside food for the Vaiśvadeva, he should give alms. But one who is widowed (or without a wife) should perform the sprinkling around the cooking fire, offer the food with the Vyāhṛtis, and then perform the Śakalahoma with the hymn beginning "devakṛtasyainasaḥ" and others. Then, having offered the food with the mantra "prajāpataye svāhā," he should present the Kākabali and worship the lunar day (tithi). Apart from this, he should not perform anything else.

He should always eat only vighasa, or observe the Cāndrāyaṇa fast. Vighasa is that which remains after being eaten; likewise, what remains from a sacrifice is amṛta. He who eats otherwise consumes nothing but sin.

One cooks here for a specific reason; for this eating of what is left over is prescribed as the food of the virtuous. There is also a Vedic revelation (śruti): "He who eats alone becomes solely a vessel of sin. Having reflected on this, one should eat after having performed the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña).
[Now follows the rule for eating. (l4.)

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having washed his feet and sipped water, he shall sit facing the east in a clean, enclosed place that has been well-smeared and swept. Having anointed himself with holy perfumes and wearing golden purifiers (*pavitra*), and holding a *pavitra* without knots, he shall offer salutation (*upasthāna*) with the words "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ Om" as the food is being brought forth. He shall restrain his speech. The food set out [is offered] with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*): "To Bhūḥ, to Agni, to the Earth, and to the Great One, Svāhā! To Bhuvaḥ, to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, and to the Great One, Svāhā!"

*Suvar ādityāya ca dive ca mahate ca svāhā!* *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svar candramase nakṣatrebhyaś ca digbhyaś ca mahate ca svāhā!* Having sprinkled water clockwise, one should offer a portion of the first morsel of food as a *bali* offering from the meal. To the south of oneself: *Namaḥ dharmarājāya*, *namaḥ citraguptāya*, *namaḥ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*. "Wherever they may dwell, for the satisfaction of those beings whose selves are afflicted by hunger and thirst, let this water be [an offering]."

Saying "as is comfortable," he places the vessel down toward the northwest, touches it with his left hand, and drinks water while reciting, "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*).

Then, having eaten the food without touching his teeth and without it coming into contact with his lips, he offers the oblations into the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) using the five successive formulas beginning with, "O Prāṇa, enter me, do not burn me, [I offer] this to thee, svāhā.

The oblation to *prāṇa* is made with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger; the oblation to *apāna* with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger; and the oblation to *vyāna* with the thumb, ring finger, and little finger.

The *udāna* oblation is offered with the thumb, middle finger, ring finger, and little finger; the *samāna* oblation is offered with all the fingers. Having set aside the vessel and washed one's hands, one should eat from a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material. (L5) Meditating on Prajāpati in the mind, one should not utter speech until the meal is finished. If one should utter speech in the interval, one should eat after muttering "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ. Upon seeing hair, nails, insects, excrement, or the like, one should remove a clod of earth from that spot, scatter ashes over it, and [sprinkle] water again. (P47b., f45a., l1)

Having sprinkled [the food] with water, one should consume what has been commended by word. One should eat sweet food first, then liquids in the middle, and solids last; finally, one should again eat liquids.

Eating in this manner, one is released from [diseases of] strength and health. If there is thirst for water during the meal, one should drink from a vessel held in the left hand without letting go of the food-vessel with the right hand. At the time of serving, everything—rice, salt, condiments, and so forth—should be given with a ladle. Raw items or those cooked in oil should be given by hand. All items such as garlic, onions, and the like...

[The following] is to be avoided: (l3. all [fruits] such as the plantain (*kadali*) and the *kāravalli* are to be accepted. Milk during the day is to be avoided; curd and *tintriṇī* at night are to be avoided.

One should not eat any food—whether cakes, tubers, roots, fruits, or meat—with the teeth. Therefore, one should be well-satisfied. Having thus eaten thirty-two morsels silently (l4.), and having drunk [water] at the end with the hands unwashed, saying "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), [one drinks] the remainder of half what was drunk. With the mantra [... for those dwelling in the lotuses and *arbudas* in the meritorious abode of Raurava.

"May the water given to those in need become inexhaustible. With these words, he should dismiss [the offerings] at the edge of the *bali*. Having thrown the circular *pavitra* into the vessel, he should not touch the vessel again. Moving elsewhere and sitting down, he should perform sixteen mouthfuls of rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*) on his left side. Having washed both hands with earth, he should clean his teeth with wooden sticks, as well as his knees and feet. Then, having washed his hand and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice, he should wipe his hand and rinse it thoroughly with both thumbs.

Having cast [the food] into the eyes, having touched the eyes, having touched fire, and having remembered his chosen deity, he should remember Śayyātī, Sukanyā, Acyavana, Śakra, and the two Aśvins. He whose memory recalls these immediately after eating—his sight shall never fail. Having thus remembered, he gazes at the region of the heart, saying: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter into the limbs; swell with this food. Having sipped water again, he lets his hand flow over the big toe of his right foot, saying: "The Person is the size of a thumb, and the thumb..."

"Having taken refuge [in Him], the Lord of the entire world... [He] satisfies [all], the Eater of All. With the mantra for the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantra*), he should perform the rite with his hands raised. Having recited the five successive formulas beginning with "Entering into faith and breath, may you swell with the food of the immortal oblation offered into the breath," and "Entering into the downward breath (*apāna*)," etc., he should join [the breaths] with the syllable "Brahman is my self for the sake of immortality. Wherever one eats, there one should collect the remnants, remove them elsewhere, and smear that spot with cow dung.

Those in which cooking has been performed are "prepared" (*kṛta*); these are without mantras. Having mixed together the *annalepas* (rice-smeared fragments) and *vyañjanalepas* (vegetable-smeared fragments) from them, having scraped them off with a piece of wood or similar tool, and having blended them with water, one should pour them out in the northern part of the house with the mantra, "O Rudras, those who are here... When this is done, the site (*vāstu*) becomes auspicious. [Recite: "May this food be for my strength, and for Agni, Nila, and Parā. May it be transformed for me; may there be unimpeded happiness. [May it be] for Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, as well as Udāna and Vyāna. Food..."

May it be nourishing; may there be for me unimpeded happiness. May Agasti, Agniṣvātta, and Anala digest entirely the food eaten by me, and may that result in my well-being. May [the Lord] grant me freedom from disease... May Viṣṇu, the Blessed One, who alone is the primordial source of all senses, bodies, and embodied beings—by that truth, may this entire food, bestowing health upon me, reach its full digestion.
Just as food is colored by Viṣṇu and its transformation occurs through fate,
by that truth may this meal of mine be digested.
Having uttered this, he should, with his own hand, [offer] the *paridodhara* [water];
being untiring, he should perform the task that bestows ease.

Then, having given betel-leaf to the twice-born, he should chew it. (L5. Thus, when the fifth part of the day has passed, he should spend the sixth and seventh parts with the study of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. In the eighth...
The outward twilight ritual (*bahissandhyā*), however, occurs after that;
when the sun has reached the western mountain peak, one should perform the outward twilight ritual outside, provided with the washing of the feet, holding *kuśa* grass in hand, and composed in mind.

Sitting by the water's edge and performing the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), [one should say]: "For the destruction of my accumulated sins and for the pleasure of the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall perform the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃ-sandhyā*). As before, [recite] *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and so forth. For the section beginning with *agniśca*, Sūrya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Agni is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the sipping of water. "May Agni and wrath, and whatever sin I have committed during the day—may they take it away. I offer this in the light of Truth; *svāhā*. Having sipped water three times, the remainder is as before. However, there are three offerings of water (*arghya*). While still seated...

One should perform [the ritual] on the ground. Then, one should perform the *prāyaścitta-arghya*, the *brahmāstra*, the consecration of weapons (*astrasaṃskāra*), and all other rites as before. Having performed the salutation, [one proceeds] as before at the place of recitation.

Having performed the invocation of the Gāyatrī and so forth, and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times as before, one should dismiss the Gāyatrī after the appearance of the stars. "I shall perform the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃ-sandhyopasthāna*). For the mantra *imaṃ me*: Śunaśśepa is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*); Varuṇa is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is in the worship of the Sun. *Imaṃ me...* [etc.]
O Varuṇa, hear us today and be gracious; we seek you for protection. Approaching you with prayer and adoration, the sacrificer desires this through his oblations:

O Varuṇa, be mindful of us here without anger; do not steal away our common life from us. Whatever law of yours we violate day by day, as people do, or whatever offense against the divine host we humans commit here through thoughtlessness—O God, do not harm us because of that sin.

"O gods, whether [the gambler] has cheated at dice in play or whether he knows the truth, may all that be as loose as a withered reed; O Varuṇa, may we be those who offer you our service. (L3) Having performed [the rites] as before, having paid homage to Śiva and the other deities, and having gone home, washed his feet, and sipped water, he performs the *aupāsana* oblation: "To Agni, svāhā! To Agni, this [is offered]. "To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Prajāpati, this [is offered]. (L4) He should perform the remainder as before. The religious student (*brahmacārī*) acts as in the morning rite. But the widower (*vidhura*), after the principal oblation—

He should act like a householder. Having performed the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) as before, he should not perform the offering for dogs and crows. Some, however, say that after performing the *vaiśvadeva-homa*, one should not perform the offering of oblations nor the offering for dogs and crows. At the first watch, he should eat together with guests who have arrived at that time, as well as his dependents, sons, and others, as previously described. He should smear the area where the food remains with ashes and sprinkle it with water. Some [say] regarding the remnants... in the chapters and at the evening twilights.

They practice a reduction in the recitation of the *gāyatrī*. And they say: "On the fourth, eighth, ninth, fourteenth, and lunar days (*tithi*), the recitation shall be half of the daily [norm]; on the seventh, thirty-seven; on the new moon day (*pratipad*), thirty-six; likewise on the two festival days (*parvan*); on the tenth, ten less three; and on this [fifteenth], twenty. Thus it is at all times beginning with the Viṣṭi; in the evening it is thus, but not so in the morning. Or rather, it should be done in that manner after having taken food and having chewed betel.

Having washed his feet, taken four mouthfuls of water for rinsing, and sipped water; having ascended the bed, having spread it out, and having gone to the center; having placed a bamboo staff near the head of the bed, and having set down a water-vessel near the head and lit a lamp; having sat upon a soft bed provided with a pillow, with his head toward the east or the south, and having recollected his chosen deity; [he should] recite the *trisūkta*.
"Depart, O serpent; may it be well with you. Go far away, O highly illustrious one, remembering the words of Astika at the conclusion of Janamejaya’s sacrifice.
Agastya, Madhava, and the mighty Mucukunda [are my protectors]."
Kapila, Muni, Astika, and Pañca—these five sleep in comfort.

From Jaratkāru and Jaratkārū was born the highly illustrious Jaratkāru, who is true to his promise; may he protect me from the serpents. (*Brahmacāridharma*) Salutations to you, O Narmadā; salutations again and again to Narmadā.
"Salutations to you, O Narmadā; protect me from the poisonous serpent! Having thus recited this, one should devote the final two watches of the night to the study of the Vedas.
By spending those two watches in [meditation], one becomes fit for union with Brahman.

At the time of approaching his own wife, however, during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), he should avoid perfumes, ointments, betel, and the like; he should avoid the fourth, sixth, eighth, and eleventh lunar days, as well as festival days and the day of a *śrāddha* ceremony. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītin*), remaining silent, and having extinguished the lamp, he should approach her. If, however, he should approach her outside of her fertile period, he should then perform the rite of the "constructed back" (*pṛṣṭhanirmita*). The couple should remain unclothed [during this].

He should go to bed. One who desires a virtuous son, however, should engage in sexual intercourse with his own wife during the latter part of the night. Having done so, the two of them should go outside, perform purification by urination, apply ashes, and then sleep.
[The Duties of a Student]

Outside the monastery, there is purification, ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), bathing, the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), service to the sacred fire, the fetching of sacrificial fuel, residence in the teacher’s household, and the study of the Vedas; likewise, the midday twilight devotion, the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the libation to the ancestors (*nityatarpaṇa*), the practice of begging for alms, service to the teacher, the evening twilight devotion, service to the sacred fire, subsisting on alms-food, sleeping on the ground, and study during the final watch of the night following the evening. This concludes the duties of the *snātaka*.

A religious student (*brahmacārin*), however, must observe these rules as a matter of necessity. Regarding those rules: he shall wear a single sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); he shall carry a loincloth, a black antelope skin as an upper garment, ashes, and rudrākṣa beads; he shall wear a girdle of muñja grass, hold a palāśa staff, and carry a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). His lower garment shall be a hemless cloth (*khaṇḍapāsa*). He shall wear a purifier (*pavitra*) and subsist solely on alms according to proper conduct. If he receives more alms than he knows how to consume, or more than he has been instructed to take, he should either bury it in the ground or cast it into the water. Every day he must fetch sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and perform the rite of placing it upon the fire. [He must abstain from] betel-leaf and sexual intercourse.

Avoiding honey, meat, liquor, women in childbirth, and the like, he should perform everything as enjoined by his teacher until his return home from studentship (*āsamāvartanāt*). Salutation to Bodhāyana.
[Now follows the duty of the *snātaka*.]
Now, the Snātaka should wear an undergarment, an upper garment, and carry a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water; he should also wear two sacrificial threads.

The turban, the deerskin, the upper garment, sandals, the parasol, the *aupāsana* fire, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and the seasonal sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*); the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails; his mode of livelihood—whether from Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or chariot-makers; wearing the *mauli* [turban]; or subsisting on alms while remaining silent—he should perform these. And he should perform all the rites for prosperity (*bhūtikarma*) connected to the gods and ancestors, consisting of the forms of the *pākayajña*, according to this rule, for Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin. Thus the supreme sages have reached the highest limit. [Householder’s Duties]

They proceed as follows: after the *samāvartana* ceremony; or, if by chance an obstacle to marriage arises, until remarriage; this is the duty toward the gods. Or, for as long as one lives, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the *aupāsana* fire every morning and evening with the *vyāhṛtis*. Everything else is the same. (l2.
[The Duties of the Householder]
Being diligent,

he should perform the twilight ablutions, silent recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, worship of the deities, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, hospitality toward guests, and the offering of water according to his ability.
A twice-born man should always perform virtuous deeds with a pure mind;
he should avoid emptiness, falsehood, deceit, lust, anger, and likewise what is merely pleasant,
as well as hatred, attachment, malice toward others, and improper action.
Dancing and singing, agriculture along with cattle-rearing, trade, and the manufacture of salt are [the occupations].
Truthful action, faith, wisdom, renunciation, and gratitude—
one who possesses these qualities is called a preeminent householder.
For a human being who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and, after death, finds Me as his goal.
Performing the entirety of the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life, and making that his supreme goal,
he attains knowledge in that very birth and goes to the auspicious state of Śiva.

"Sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, likewise studying and teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these are the six duties to be performed day by day," [says] Bodhāyana.

"Constantly using water [for purification], constantly wearing the sacred thread, constantly engaged in Vedic study, avoiding the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaching his wife during her season according to rule, and offering oblations according to the injunctions— a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world."
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to the study of the Vedas,
and having conquered his senses according to his own class, he should diligently procreate offspring.
By the study of the Vedas he honors the sages, and by the Soma sacrifice, Indra.
And by means of progeny, he has discharged his debt to the ancestors of old and rejoices in heaven.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one enjoys bliss;
and through the grandson of a son, one may cause even the celestial realm to be ascended.
[He delivers] seven descendants, seven ancestors, six others, and himself as the seventh.
By obtaining a virtuous son, one becomes a deliverer from sin.
For he who is devoted to the welfare of his parents, intent on the well-being of cows and Brahmins,
a performer of sacrifices, and a devotee of the gods, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
He constantly pursues the three aims of life and worships the deities.
One should perform this daily and constantly; one should always pay homage to the gods.

One who is constantly devoted to the practice of discernment, endowed with patience, and compassionate is declared a true householder; one does not become a householder merely by living in a house. Furthermore, he should perform his duties according to his capacity and avoid actions that are censurable.
Having shaken off the turbidity of delusion and attained the unsurpassed yoga,
A householder is released from bondage; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
By offering funeral oblations, he honors the ancestors, and likewise the gods and guests through his duties.
Through internal [meditation], sages, and the study of sacred texts, he honors Prajāpati through his offspring.
By performing his duties, he protects all beings; through his affection, he protects the entire world.
A person attains worlds gathered through his own actions,
just as all rivers and streams find their station in the ocean;
in the same way, all [ascetics] reach their final resting place in the householder.
And for all of these, according to the injunctions of the Vedas and the Smṛtis, [this applies].
O best of men, he who performs the rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti without a waist-string (kaṭisūtra) is called a householder in name only; for he truly possesses only three eyes.

One should know that nothing is fruitless; even he is "naked," according to the sacred tradition. A flower on the ear, a thread on the hip, and [the body] wrapped in a garment—[these constitute his attire].
If a foolish soul, excluded from all sacred rites, should wear [the sacred thread]—
even one whose top-knot is already tied— if he performs a rite that touches the tip of his crest, he would be like one carrying a cooking pot upon his head.
That action should be known as fruitless which is performed with the knees outside;
likewise, at the time of performing the rite, the navel and the two joints of the knees [should not be exposed].
Having covered himself with a cloth, the wise man should perform his duties without sloth;
O brahmins, he should wear the tail of a tortoise as a sacred thread and an upper garment.
One should perform the daily rites with self-restraint and a pure mind.
An upper garment should be worn by a twice-born man, just like the sacred thread.
One should wear it around the waist during prostration, libation, fire sacrifice, and bathing;
furthermore, one should not converse with eunuchs, heretics, outcasts, barbarians, and the like.
He should not even look at them; if he must look, he should gaze at the sun.

If there are other women in the city, he should speak with them only so much as is necessary for conversation in a secluded place, and he should speak only what ought to be said. He should not converse with Caṇḍālas, Ambaṣṭhas, washermen, and the like during the night, nor should he listen to their speech. He should not converse with Śūdras in vain; if he must converse, he should do so wearing the *nivīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder). This refers to the case of unworthy Śūdras.
Having walked outside, he should wash his feet and enter the house.

Having entered the house of a Śūdra, he should bathe again before entering his own home. He should not teach the Dharma to a Śūdra, nor should he impart mantras to atheists and the like. He should perform acts such as giving gifts to and receiving them from the learned, as well as conversing with them; however, he should avoid spending time in their company. He should avoid sleeping during the day and approaching his wife [during her period]. He should never remain impure.

One should not eat while hearing the sound of drums, oil-presses, or the noise of chariot processions. One should not climb to the top of a tree, nor should one ascend a mountain. One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms. One should not cast off the body out of despair. In every way, one should protect oneself. During the day, one should avoid covering the head after finishing the acts of urination and defecation. One should not discharge urine, feces, or spittle into water. One should not walk about displaying one's private parts in water. One should not remain naked even for a moment. One should not cut fruits and the like with one's fingernails.

One should not look at a naked person, nor at one who is naked, nor at those engaged in sexual intercourse; if one should see them, one should look at the sun. One should not wash one's feet, nor bathe. One should not dance, nor sing. One should not cut one's nails or hair. One should not break a clod of earth, nor cut grass. One should not play with dice, nor look at feces or urine.
One should not splash water with the foot or the hand. One should not wash one foot with the other. One should not sleep during the two twilights, nor travel, nor perform household chores.

One should not eat what has been prepared for oneself; with awareness, one should not kill worms, insects, and the like. One should not engage in quarrels with learned men or with elders such as one's father. Upon sneezing, one should say "May you live a hundred years"; upon stumbling, one should take some dust and place it on one's forehead. Upon yawning, one should avoid it by snapping one's fingers. Performing daily and occasional rites without indolence, and avoiding what is forbidden, the wise man shall find happiness in this world and the next.
[Now follows the procedure for oil massage.]
An oil massage (abhyaṅga) is recommended on the days of the week of Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn; likewise,
the four [days] beginning with the second, as well as the seventh,
the ninth, the tenth, and the thirteenth are traditionally held to be auspicious.
A wise person seeking happiness should likewise avoid anointing and bathing during the nights of Uttaraphalgunī, Śravaṇa, and Ārdrā.

There is no fault even on a prohibited day, such as Saturday; this is the rule for anointing (*abhyañjana*). It should be avoided during the morning and evening hours, because of the recollection of the faults [associated with those times]. For children, the elderly, and the sick, there is no such restriction. There is no fault even if the oil is mixed with the essence of food or substances. One should have the massage and anointing performed by the hand of another.

[The person receiving the massage] should face either the east or the south; one should not perform it while facing west or north. Having sat down and had the anointing performed, at the conclusion, [one should honor] the one who performed it.
He touches his hands [with the mantra]: "O Indra, bestow strength upon our bodies; O Indra, protect our bodies. Bestow strength upon your son for his life, for you are the giver of strength.

The response is: "I am [so-and-so]. Therefore, one should not have it performed by a Śūdra or others. At the end of winter, there should be one *ghaṭikā*; in the cool season (*śiśira*), three *ghaṭikās*. One should dwell [in water] for five *nāḍikās* in summer, and likewise six *nāḍikās*. During the rainy season and the autumn season, one should perform the bath immediately (*sadyasnāna*).
[Now, the time for shaving.]

All months are times for shaving, except for Śuci, Nabhasya, Sahas, and Tapas, which should be avoided. The days of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Moon bring auspiciousness for shaving. The days of the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are to be avoided for shaving.
On the day of a malefic planet and so forth, or on an auspicious day for Brahmins when the sun is favorable.
For Kṣatriyas, forbearance is heroic; for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is likewise gradual.
On Mondays, the moon is auspicious during the bright fortnight, but it is censured during the dark fortnight.
One should perform [the rite] under a constellation that does not require shaving, on the days of Mercury and the Moon.
Even Brahmā does not live for a year under Mūla and Anurādhā.
The second, the third, the fifth, the seventh, as well as the tenth, the eleventh, and the thirteenth are likewise honored.
The twelfth is declared to be middling; the remainder one should avoid.
Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, Hastā, the two Aśvins, Pauṣṇa, Āditya, and Vaiṣṇava;
Mṛgaśīrṣa and Puṣya are highly recommended for the act of shaving;
Svātī, Śatabhiṣaj, Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttarās are declared to be middling for shaving; one should avoid all other [asterisms].
Cancer, Virgo, Libra, Pisces, Capricorn, Taurus, and Aquarius are auspicious.
The rest, however, should always avoid the [specified] zodiac signs for the act of shaving;

likewise, one should know how to perform the purification of garlands and so forth from the body. Having had his hair, nails, and beard clipped, he should become a householder among the ranks of women.
[The Ritual for Shaving]

Having performed that [rite] at dawn, he should summon a barber and sit in a secluded place facing either east or north, until the sounding of conchs and other musical instruments has ceased. Having become *nivītī* (wearing the sacred thread around his neck), and having placed the barber facing him while touching a water vessel until the end [of the rite], he should shave [the hair], avoiding the three tufts on the forearm. First the root of the right arm, then the root of the left arm, and afterwards from below the throat down to the navel.

One should shave from the back of the head down to the waist; then the beard, the top-knot (*śikhā*), and the hair within the nostrils; then all the hair on the right side and so forth; then the private parts; then the right foot, and then the left foot. In this manner one should have the hair shaved. Thereafter, one should clip the nails. If the act of shaving is performed on a day forbidden during periods of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like, one must have it shaved again on a subsequent day that is declared auspicious. When done in this way, there is an increase in longevity. Since this is a rite for the prolongation of life (*āyuṣyakarman*), it should be performed after due deliberation.

Then, having gone to a river or similar place and bathed, one should put on fresh clothes again and perform a clay-bath (*mṛttikā-snāna*). Then, having performed thirteen immersions (*nimajjana*), and having completed the ritual bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth, one should discard the wet garment and put on dry clothing. One should then bathe once more as previously described. In the absence of dry clothing, one should wring out the wet garment, shake it seven times, display it in the sunlight, and then put it on again before bathing. When this has been done, one becomes fit for the ritual action.
|| Now, the Duties of Women ||
She should perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties with devotion;
thus, being ever agreeable, she shall always be dear to her husband.

While her husband is still unawakened, she herself, having first awakened him, goes outside and disposes of her bodily impurities and so forth. Having performed the purification (*śauca*) instructed by her husband, having cleansed her teeth, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), she sprinkles the house with cow-dung water, sweeps it, performs a neck-bath (*kaṇṭhasnāna*) in a river or similar body of water, puts on her garment, applies a coating of turmeric and other substances, pays homage to the Sun, and recites the mantra instructed by her husband. Then, having returned home and performed tasks such as fetching water, [she proceeds].

Having performed the service at the *agnihotra* or the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), and having carried out the washing of utensils and other such tasks; having given that food—which was kept in a vessel for the protection of children and others—to the children and others; and having decorated the house, she should thereafter cook with side-dishes for the sake of the deities. Then, after the offering to the deities, the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, the *bali* offerings, the honoring of guests, and the feeding of her husband and children, she should eat. She should eat whatever is pleasing to her husband and avoid what is not pleasing. At evening time, she should decorate the house.

(l5. Having lit a lamp, and having performed the evening *agnihotra* or *aupāsana* rites, the *vaiśvadeva* and *baliharaṇa* offerings, and so forth, as well as the worship of the lunar day (*tithi*), the feeding of her husband, and the feeding of the children, she should attend to these duties. She herself should eat what remains. When her husband has fallen asleep, she herself should sleep. (p56a., f53b., l1. When her husband is eager for pleasure, she should act in accordance with his desire. When he is delighted, she should be delighted; when he is distressed, she should be distressed; when he is away on a journey, she should wear soiled garments; when he has eaten, she should have eaten; when he has fasted, she should fast; and when he is angry, [she should be likewise].

A woman who is afraid that her husband might die from drinking [something] will die herself if he does not drink it. The husband alone is her deity; she should not perform fasts, vows, or similar observances. If she should perform them, she must do so by the command of her husband. At the time of eating, she should say, "Homage to Jyeṣṭhā," and after having eaten some food, she should offer a small portion as an oblation (*bali*) to Jyeṣṭhā.
Actions such as anointing with oil, body massage, brushing the teeth, combing the hair, wearing clothes, sleeping, eating, vomiting, and adorning the body should be performed [only] for the husband.
When seeing [such things], one should not act; by such means as these, one attains heaven. [Now follows the duty of widows.]
Any woman who, upon her husband's death, maintains the state of widowhood anywhere, shall regain her husband and enjoy the delights of heaven. (L.
4) …The binding of the husband’s hair-braid results in the bondage of the husband.
Therefore, a widow must likewise act with her head [shaved].
One should always take food only once, never a second time;
one may observe the vow for three nights, or five nights, or even the fortnightly vow;
one may perform the month-long fast, the half-month fast, or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should perform the Kṛcchra, the Parāka, or even the Taptakṛcchra penance,
subsisting on barley, or on fruits, or on vegetables, or on milk, or on ghee.
She should maintain her life-sustenance only until she herself reaches the place of breaking her fast;
if a woman who has made the vow of celibacy (*paryaṅka*) is a widow, she causes her husband to fall [from heaven].
Therefore, desiring her husband's happiness, she should sleep on the ground;
a widow must never, under any circumstances, apply ointments to her limbs.
Every day, one should perform the libation for the husband with water mixed with kusha grass and sesame seeds;
likewise for his father and his grandfather, preceded by their names and gotras.
The worship of the deity must be performed with the thought that he is her husband, and not otherwise;
she should always meditate upon her husband alone as the supreme deity bearing a divine form.

In this way, even a widow who is perpetually devoted to the highest conduct is considered auspicious. She may perform recitation (*japa*) after bathing like a *śūdra*; for me, there is no [distinction between] *draviṇa* and *mathava*. And the lighting of the lamp is prescribed through the husband’s intent and not otherwise.
And the recitation of her mantra is prescribed by means of Vedic rites for one who has mastered the vital breaths.
That woman who, while her husband is alive, remains established in celibacy,
attains heaven upon death, just like those lifelong celibates.

For as long as life lasts, she shall perform the ritual touching of water for the deceased, eat but one meal a day, sleep on the ground, observe celibacy, and abstain from pungent salts, honey, and meat. When the sun has risen, she should perform her duties such as bathing. On occasions such as pilgrimages, she should go together with her sons and others; having performed the bathing and other rites with them, she should have them perform the long-term *śrāddha*, giving of gifts, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth.
For as long as she lives, being devoted to hearing the Dharma and chanting the Name, when she dies, she will attain heaven and subsequently reunite with her husband. [Thus it is said.]

The section on daily rites (*nityakarman*) is completed in the *Karmaprakāśikā*, composed by the venerable Pañcākṣara-gurunātha, born of the lineage of the Ācārya Jñānaśiva, the ornament of the Kāśyapa clan. Homage to the venerable Gurus. May there be auspiciousness; here begins the *Bodhāyanamantrapraśna*.
I bow to the lords of the quarters, who bestow the fruits of all desires;
may they make my actions fruitful and may they constantly perform what is auspicious.
I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the divine ministrant of the sacrifice,
the invoker who bestows the most excellent treasures—
golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver.
O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who is radiant.
O Jātavedas, bring that Lakṣmī who never departs,
through whom I may find gold, cows, horses, and men.

I invoke the goddess Śrī, who has horses at her front, a chariot in her midst, and elephants as her attendants; may the goddess Śrī be pleased with me. I invoke you here, O Śrī: you who have a golden smile, a golden rampart, who are moist, radiant, satisfied, and bestowing satisfaction; you who dwell upon a lotus, possessing the color of a lotus.
O God, I take refuge in her who is moon-like, radiant, blazing with glory, the noble Fortune cherished by the world—her whose rim is marked by lotuses; may my misfortune perish, for I choose you.
O you who possess the luster of the sun, born from austerity, may this bilva tree, the lord of the forest,
drive away from me through its fruits the power of illusion, as well as misfortune that is base and external. O Lord, may you approach me along with fame and with Manu.
I have become manifest in this kingdom; may that grant me an increase in fame.
May I destroy this inauspicious Lakṣmī who is stained by hunger and thirst; may you drive away from my home all misfortune and lack of prosperity.
[I worship] her who has the senses as her gate, who is invincible, eternally nourishing, and bestowing abundance.
I invoke you, Śrī, the sovereign of all beings.
May we obtain the desire of the mind and the intention of speech;
may we attain the essence of cattle, the form of food, and may glory be established upon us.
O Kardama, you who have become manifest through the primordial mud, arise from that mud!
Dwell in my family, O Śrī, the mother garlanded with lotuses;
let the waters release their moisture, and may she take delight in the house of the Vasu.
O Jātavedas, bring to my family my own goddess, my mother Śrī— moist, lotus-born, nourishing, golden-hued, and wearing a golden garland;
bring to me Sūryā, the golden Lakṣmī.
She was moist, capable of performing sacrifices, a sacrificial post, tawny-hued, and adorned with a garland of lotuses.
O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who is radiant;
O Jātavedas, bring to me that Lakṣmī who never departs.
May I [obtain] her in whom there is abundant gold, cattle, slaves, horses, and many men.
O beloved of the lotus, O lotus-like one, O you who hold a lotus in your hand, O you whose abode is the lotus, O you with eyes as broad as lotus petals!
O beloved of the universe, O you who are agreeable to the mind of Viṣṹṇu, O you who consist of wisdom, may your lotus-feet be present here.
We know the Great Goddess; we meditate upon the Consort of Viṣṇu.
May she inspire us.
O Indra, Maghavan, those deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at all the Soma-pressings— those which you performed for the one who presses the juice,
when you opened up the wealth of the Pārāvata, the Puru, and the Sṛd for Śarabha.

May that Lord, the God who is the master of breath, who wears a skin as his garment, who wields the Pināka bow, and who is the Brahmā who brought forth Brahmā—that Īśāna bestows long life upon us; to him I offer an oblation of clarified butter.
Shining from the midst of his body, the radiant one, the Gharma, has come;
may that god, for the sake of life, consume the clarified butter that destroys the snares of death.
He is the light of Brahman, the embryo placed within the wives of Brahman, who brings forth many forms.
Having honored the Sun, who is worthy of worship and who holds the golden plantain tree, we increase his lifespan with clarified butter.

I worship Śrī, Lakṣmī, Abalā, Ambikā, Gā, and Ṣaṣṭhī; they say that one should not neglect them. We satisfy that beautiful Vidyā, the source of Brahman, here for the sake of longevity with clarified butter.
The daughters of Dakṣa, belonging to all wombs, of noble birth, numbering in the thousands, possessing every form and diverse in appearance.

May those sons, the well-winged ones who rise at dawn, the life-sustaining ones, enjoy this offering. May the divine hosts, manifold in form and ancient, not cut short our lifespan and protect our heroes.
To them I offer oblations in many ways with clarified butter; do not harm my progeny or my spirit... the Virāj...
One was here in the beginning from whom this world arose, the guardian of the universe;
into whom the world also enters—that god has indeed separated [all things] here for our long life.

Having offered clarified butter, we have magnified the Vasus, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Ṛbhus, the Yakṣas, the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Viśvedevas, the serpents, and all the Aṅgirases, for the sake of our own long life. O Viṣṇu, grant us your closest protection; he strikes away [evil] from us.

May he pour forth a stream of honey, yielding inexhaustible abundance. Be gracious to the earth, O radiant one, for the one who praises you. May he who grants us protection extend it wide. He is wondrous; let him bestow wondrous wealth upon us.

O most wonderful one, awaken for us a most wonderful sovereignty, a bright, abundant wealth of many heroes, and great splendor; may you be renowned through your shining rays. We take hold of King Soma, Varuṇa, Agni, the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the Brahman. O Brahman, you are the Brahman; homage to you! O Brahman, homage to the Brahman! You are Varuṇa, whose vows are firm; you belong to Varuṇa. O Jātavedas, being yoked, carry [the oblation] forward; O Agni, know this rite as it is being performed. You are the physician.
The performer of the supreme remedy, you have made the mind [your] horse for this rite. May auspicious deeds come to us from every side—unfailing, unassailable, and bursting open with strength.
O gods, so that we may be united on the chariot, may those protectors who extend their aid day by day [be with us]. O Virūpākṣa, do not oppress me; do not bind me; you have already oppressed me.
They call you the son of Nirṛti; accomplish our rites for us. O Virūpākṣa, great sacrificer, [seize] the one who strikes his own kin, the one with a speckled belly—he who is this [one] toward me...

May there be eternal prosperity and nourishment for him whom you, O Giver of Wealth, obstruct. When you descend crosswise, saying "I am the supporter," I worship you with a stream of clarified butter, O Goddess who brings about success.
To the gods who are propitious, to the divine ones who are successful; [and] to Agni, who is without guile and without reproach—[I offer this]. You are truth, you are reality; you are without guile.

Sustained by an unguiled mind, with an unguiled [mind], carry the oblation; through you, bestow healing upon us. Whatever in this rite has been performed with a desire for reward, whether by word or by deed, all that I appease with this oblation. May the gods be satisfied; may they dwell in the springtime with clarified butter. Protect us, O Agni, with your first [form]; protect us also with your second; protect us with your threefold song, O Lord of Strength!

Protect us with your four [forms], O Vasu! Whatever in this rite has been left over or whatever was deficient here—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-offered and well-sacrificed for me.
To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the offerer of well-sacrificed oblations, for the fulfillment of the desires of the offerings. Thus ends the first chapter in the sequence of mantras of the *Ṛkkilakārikā*. 1.4.1.

May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati place the seed, and Dhātṛ establish the embryo within the prepared [womb]. As the earth has Agni as its embryo, as the sky is pregnant with Indra, and as Vāyu is the embryo of the quarters—so do you bestow an embryo upon her. May Sinīvālī grant you an embryo; may Sarasvatī grant you an embryo;
may both Aśvins and Puṣan provide you with two lotus-wreaths. O Aśvins, with golden friction-sticks churned by the hands, I place this embryo in you so that it may be born in the tenth month.
O Nejameṣa, fly away! O Suputra, fly back again! Place within this woman, who desires a son, a male embryo.

I am the earth; you are the sky. I am the Sāman; you are the Ṛc. For we two are united here; let us pour our seed together for the sake of a male son, one who knows the Vedas, for prosperity, for good offspring, and for great heroic power.
I have placed the embryo within the plants; I [have placed it] within the cattle and the worlds... I brought forth the offspring of the wise; I [placed] sons within the wombs.
O Pūṣan, impel you toward her who is most auspicious, in whom men sow the seed—she who desires to spread apart her thighs for us, so that we may strike our phallus upon her.

O Prajāpati, fashioning me, may you accept me; together with Tvaṣṭṛ, with the gods, and with Indra, rejoicing with all the gods and the Arātis, may we be mothers of many sons. "Soma alone rules over us," so say the Brāhmaṇas regarding offspring. Sitting with wheels turned away, that one of yours has stretched out across the distance. From limb after limb arise; from the heart he is born. You are indeed the self named "son"; live for a hundred autumns! Become a stone, become an axe, become gold as your armor. With my hand, I smell you, the protector of cattle—[Name]!

May Vāyu protect your back today, and may the Aśvins [protect] your sides. May Savitṛ protect you while you are making yourself visible; may Bṛhaspati protect you from the garment you have put on, and may the Viśvedevas protect you from behind. O Waters, while men sleep, remain awake; drive away the Rākṣasas. Homage, homage to the non-terrible and the terrible! To the one who causes entry, the one who causes complete entry, the one with the wide mouth, the curious one, the elephant-like one, the paralyzing one, the deluding one, and to Kṛṣṇā, Viśākhā, Vimalā, Brahmarātri, and those numbered among the rivals.

"May those [missiles] fall infallible; homage, homage indeed to those Mothers! "I send you forth, O ocean-like ones, as imperishable; go back to your own source. May I be unharmed in my progeny; let this milk not be spilled. O Jṛṃhiṇī, grant us well-being; may the Aśvins fashion it for us. May the divine Aditi, Bhaga, and Anirvaṇa grant well-being. May Pūṣan, the Asura, bestow well-being; may Heaven and Earth with their gracious mind grant well-being. For the sake of well-being we invoke Vāyu; Soma is well-being, he who is the lord of the world. [We invoke] Bṛhaspati with his entire host."

For our well-being, for our well-being, O Ādityas and Soma, be present with us! May all the gods today be for our well-being; may Agni Vaiśvānara, the Vasu, be for our well-being! May the divine Ṛbhus protect us for our well-being! May Rudra guard us for our well-being! O Mitra and Varuṇa, grant us well-being! O wealthy Pathyā Svasti, grant us well-being! O Indra and Agni, grant us well-being! O Aditi, bestow well-being upon us! May we follow the path of well-being, even that of the sun and the moon! Returning again, unharmed, knowing the way, come to our meeting! This is the journey for well-being.

Tārkṣya, of the unbroken wheel, the great being, the wind among the gods, the slayer of Asuras, the friend of Indra in battles—him we invoke like a ship for our protection. Aṃhomuc, the conqueror of the Aṅgirasas, Svastyātreya, and Tārkṣya in my mind—with hands uplifted, I seek refuge in him. May he be our well-being; may he grant us fearlessness in adversities.
O bird, you who have been proclaimed from birth as one who utters auspicious speech like a boat for Aditi—may you be a bringer of good fortune; may no one come against you, and may everyone find you.

May the eagle not seize you with his beak; may no arrow-bearing hero strike you from behind. May he place you in the direction of the ancestors, O most auspicious one, speaking what is favorable here.

Cut down from the south of our houses, O bird of auspicious omen, you who speak of blessings! Do not be a bringer of misfortune, nor one who desires evil; may we, possessed of brave sons, speak aloud and establish ourselves in prosperity.
Catching hold from the right, the birds cry out their song according to the seasons. Both voices sound forth like Sāman-singers chanting the Gāyatra hymn; he shines resplendent among the people.

Like an *udgātṛ* priest, O bird, you sing the *sāman*; like a son of the *brahman*, you recite at the libations. As a bull, you have bellowed; our thought is full of vigor.
